META.subject: Essential Mathematics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 2.2 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Symmetry and lines of symmetry in plane figures
• Properties of reflection using objects and their images
• Reflection on a plane surface (drawing images given an object and a mirror line)
• Reflection on a Cartesian plane (mirror lines x=0, y=0, and y=x)
• Drawing the mirror line given an object and its image (plane surface and Cartesian plane)
• Application of reflection in real-life situations (e.g., driving mirrors, road safety, design patterns)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify lines of symmetry in plane figures,
b) determine the properties of reflection using objects and its image,
c) draw an image given an object and a mirror line on a plane surface,
d) draw an image given an object and a mirror line on a Cartesian plane,
e) draw the mirror line given an object and its image on a plane surface and a Cartesian plane,
f) apply reflection in real-life situations,
g) appreciate the role of reflection in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Learning to Learn: The learner develops relationship skills when discussing with peers the applications of reflections in real life such as use of mirrors in road transport.
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner acquires connection skills when making cut outs of plane figures for finding the number of lines of symmetry.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: The learner takes turns when working with peers to make cut outs of plane figures used in reflection activities.
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of instruments used to construct images formed after reflection in the mirror lines.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Learners question why an image in a mirror appears the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, driving inquiry into the properties of reflection.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners systematically place objects at measured distances from a plane mirror and record image positions to deduce reflection properties.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Learners measure and compare object and image distances, perpendicularity of the mirror line, and size congruence to draw evidence-based conclusions.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners use gathered evidence from plane and Cartesian-plane activities to articulate the invariant properties of reflection (congruence, perpendicular bisector relationship).
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: Learners discuss with peers and present findings on real-life applications of reflection such as driving mirrors and road safety.
UNIT.pcis: • Road Safety: The learner discusses with peers the applications of reflections in real life such as use of driving mirrors in reducing road crashes on Kenyan roads.
UNIT.careers:
• Architecture and Interior Design: Reflection symmetry is used in designing buildings, floor tile patterns, and décor — relevant to construction careers prevalent across Nairobi and other urban centres.
• Road Transport and Logistics: Matatu and truck drivers rely on plane and convex mirrors; understanding reflection supports careers in vehicle operation and road safety management.
• Fashion and Textile Design: Kanga, kitenge, and Maasai shuka pattern designers use lines of symmetry and reflection to create repeating motifs.
• Photography and Media: Photographers and videographers use mirror reflections for composition; media technology students benefit from understanding image formation.
• Sports Coaching and Recreation: Coaches use reflective analysis of athletes' movements; sports management careers at institutions such as those supporting Kenyan marathon runners benefit from spatial reasoning.
• Guidance and Counselling / Health Sciences: Body-symmetry assessments (e.g., physiotherapy) and use of diagnostic mirrors draw on knowledge of reflection.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' understanding of reflection as a geometric transformation, beginning with lines of symmetry in familiar Kenyan objects and progressing to formal constructions on plain paper and the Cartesian plane. Learners move from hands-on exploration with physical mirrors and cut-out shapes to precise geometric construction, always connecting abstract properties back to the anchoring real-world context of mirror images encountered in daily Kenyan life. Throughout the eight lessons, collaborative investigation, peer discussion, and step-by-step model building ensure that both procedural fluency and conceptual understanding of reflection are achieved.
UNIT.phenomenon: A Grade 10 learner in Nairobi notices something puzzling one morning: as she stands in front of the full-length mirror on her bedroom wall to check her school uniform, her reflection raises the opposite hand when she raises hers, yet every detail — the pattern on her Kanga skirt, the number of buttons on her shirt, the distance she stands from the glass — appears perfectly preserved. Later, on the matatu ride to school, she observes the driver constantly checking the rear-view and side mirrors; the vehicles and pedestrians visible in those mirrors are clear, life-sized representations of what is behind, yet they appear "flipped." At school, the mathematics teacher holds up a sheet of paper with a bold letter "A" printed on it and places a plane mirror beside it: the class sees a perfect mirror-image "A" in the glass — same size, same shape, but laterally reversed. Students are puzzled: Why does the image appear the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front? Why is the image the same size but "flipped"? What invisible line or rule governs where the image lands? This observable, puzzling, everyday phenomenon — the behaviour of plane mirrors — anchors the entire unit and motivates learners to uncover the precise geometric properties of reflection.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Symmetry in Kenyan leaves and national symbols: Learners collect leaves (e.g., mango, avocado, neem) from the school compound in Kisumu or Nairobi and notice that folding many leaves along their central vein produces two identical halves — raising the question of what geometric rule produces this symmetry.
• Reflections on Lake Victoria and other water bodies: Photographs taken at Lake Victoria's shore or the Nairobi Dam show perfect upside-down reflections of trees, boats, and buildings on calm water — puzzling learners about why the reflected image appears directly below the object.
• Kanga and kitenge textile patterns: Learners examine the repeating symmetric patterns on Kanga cloth sold in Mombasa markets and notice that half the pattern is a mirror image of the other half, raising questions about how designers use lines of reflection to create such patterns.
• Road safety mirrors at Kenyan junctions: Convex mirrors mounted at sharp bends on Kenyan rural roads (e.g., along the Kericho–Kisumu highway) show wide-angle reflections of oncoming traffic, prompting discussion about how the position and angle of a mirror line determines what is visible in the image.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why does a mirror show a perfect copy of the world — and where exactly does that copy live?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Symmetry Safari (Lines of Symmetry in Plane Figures): Learners are introduced to the anchoring phenomenon (the classroom plane mirror and the "flipped letter A"). They collect leaves, cut-out shapes (rectangles, squares, triangles, circles), and everyday objects (Kanga fabric swatches, bottle caps) and investigate lines of symmetry by folding and using a plane mirror. They record the number of lines of symmetry for each shape and share findings with peers, generating initial questions for the Driving Question Board.

Lesson 2 — Mirror, Mirror on the Wall (Properties of Reflection — Plane Surface): Learners stand at measured distances from a plane mirror and record the apparent distance of their image. They then use a ruler and set square to place a small object at various distances from a drawn mirror line on plain paper, locate the image, and measure: (i) object distance = image distance from mirror line; (ii) the line joining object to image is perpendicular to the mirror line; (iii) the image is congruent to the object. Learners formalise the three properties of reflection and connect them back to the anchoring phenomenon.

Lesson 3 — Drawing Images on a Plane Surface (Construction Practice): Learners use a geometrical set to construct images of given plane figures (triangles, quadrilaterals, irregular polygons) reflected in horizontal, vertical, and oblique mirror lines on plain paper. Step-by-step teacher modelling is followed by peer practice. Learners annotate each construction to label object distance, image distance, and perpendicular bisectors, reinforcing properties from Lesson 2.

Lesson 4 — Reflection on the Cartesian Plane I (x=0 and y=0): Learners plot given objects on a Cartesian plane and reflect them in the y-axis (x=0) and x-axis (y=0). They discover the coordinate rules: reflection in x=0 maps (x, y) → (−x, y); reflection in y=0 maps (x, y) → (x, −y). Learners connect these rules to the mirror-image phenomenon — the mirror line is now a coordinate axis — and practise with triangles and quadrilaterals plotted using Kenyan context coordinates (e.g., grid maps of school grounds in Nairobi).

Lesson 5 — Reflection on the Cartesian Plane II (y=x): Learners investigate reflection in the line y=x by plotting objects and their images and deducing the rule (x, y) → (y, x). They compare all three Cartesian mirror lines studied (x=0, y=0, y=x), tabulate the coordinate transformation rules, and practise mixed examples. The lesson revisits the anchoring phenomenon: just as standing closer to a physical mirror changes the image position, changing the mirror line on the Cartesian plane changes the image coordinates by a precise rule.

Lesson 6 — Finding the Mirror Line (Reverse Reflection): Given an object and its image on both a plain surface and a Cartesian plane, learners work backwards to construct or identify the mirror line (perpendicular bisector of the segment joining corresponding points). This reverse-engineering task deepens understanding of the properties of reflection. Learners connect this to the road-safety supporting phenomenon: traffic engineers determine the optimal angle and position of a junction mirror by knowing where drivers (object) and the hazard (image) must be.

Lesson 7 — Real-Life Applications and Peer Presentations: Learners investigate real-life applications of reflection in groups: (i) driving mirrors and road safety on Kenyan roads; (ii) symmetry in Kanga/kitenge design; (iii) architectural symmetry in Kenyan buildings (e.g., Parliament buildings, mosques in Mombasa). Each group prepares a short illustrated presentation linking their application to the geometric properties of reflection studied in Lessons 2–6. The Driving Question Board is updated with answers and residual questions.

Lesson 8 — Model Building, Review and Assessment: Learners produce a cumulative annotated diagram ("reflection model") that synthesises all properties and constructions: lines of symmetry, plane-surface reflection, Cartesian reflection in x=0 / y=0 / y=x, and reverse mirror-line construction. They self-assess against the KICD rubric descriptors, complete a class activity (written exercise covering all SLOs), and reflect on how the anchoring phenomenon of the everyday mirror is now fully explained by the geometric properties they have uncovered across the unit.

LESSONS.title: Symmetry Safari: Lines of Symmetry in Plane Figures

slo.purpose: To introduce the anchoring phenomenon of reflection through hands-on investigation of lines of symmetry in plane figures, and to launch the Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: Learners identify lines of symmetry in plane figures including rectangles, squares, equilateral triangles, circles, and irregular shapes such as Kanga fabric cut-outs and leaf specimens.
slo.skills: Learners make cut-outs of plane figures, fold them to locate lines of symmetry, use a plane mirror to verify symmetry, record findings in a table, and communicate observations to peers.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the presence of symmetry in everyday Kenyan objects and environments, and develop curiosity about why mirror images appear 'flipped' yet perfectly preserved.
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson of the unit. It anchors the entire storyline by presenting the puzzling phenomenon of the plane mirror and the 'flipped letter A' observed in the classroom. Learners conduct a Symmetry Safari — investigating lines of symmetry in leaves, cut-out shapes, and Kanga fabric swatches — to build the foundational concept of a line of symmetry as an invisible geometric rule that governs where a mirror image lands. Their questions and observations seed the Driving Question Board that will grow across all lessons in this unit.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners should handle scissors carefully when making cut-outs. Plane mirrors (if glass) should be handled with care to avoid breakage; acrylic mirrors are preferred. No sharp tools should be left unattended on desks.

LESSONS.overview: In this lesson, learners are introduced to the anchoring phenomenon: a Grade 10 learner in Nairobi notices that her reflection in a full-length mirror raises the opposite hand, and her mathematics teacher places a bold letter 'A' next to a plane mirror to reveal a laterally reversed image. Learners are immediately puzzled — why does the mirror produce a copy that is 'flipped'? What invisible line or rule governs this? To begin answering these questions, learners conduct a Symmetry Safari: they collect leaves from the school compound, use pre-cut paper shapes (rectangles, squares, equilateral triangles, circles), and examine Kanga fabric swatches and bottle caps. They fold and use a plane mirror to locate and count lines of symmetry, recording results in a class table. The lesson closes with learners generating initial questions for the Driving Question Board, which will be revisited and expanded across the entire unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners observe the teacher hold up a sheet of paper with a bold letter 'A' printed on it and place a plane mirror beside it. Before being told anything, learners individually write predictions in their exercise books responding to three prompts: (1) 'Draw what you think the mirror image of the letter A will look like.' (2) 'If I stand 30 cm from the mirror, how far behind the mirror do you think my image will appear? Why?' (3) 'Look at the Kanga swatch on your desk — do you think it has any lines of symmetry? How many?' Learners then share predictions in pairs (Think-Pair-Share) for 2 minutes before two or three pairs are cold-called to share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Place the letter 'A' sheet and plane mirror at the front. Say: 'Before I show you anything — look carefully and write your prediction silently. You have 90 seconds.' [WAIT 90 seconds — circulate, do NOT give hints.] 2. Display the three written prompts on the board. Read each aloud. 3. After individual writing, say: 'Now turn to your partner. Share your drawings and predictions. You have 2 minutes.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] 4. Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Amina and Kevin — what did you predict for prompt two and why?' — 'Wanjiru and Otieno — how many lines of symmetry did you predict for the Kanga swatch?' — 'Akinyi and Mwangi — what does your drawing of the mirror-A look like?' 5. Do NOT confirm or deny predictions. Say: 'Hold those predictions. We are going to gather evidence right now and see who was closest.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with written predictions. This strategy externalises prior knowledge and creates cognitive dissonance — when learners see the actual mirror image, the mismatch between prediction and observation drives curiosity and motivates the investigation. Written predictions also give the teacher a quick formative snapshot of baseline understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during individual writing and notes: (a) whether learners draw the mirror-A correctly reversed or not, (b) whether distance predictions show any proportional reasoning, (c) whether Kanga symmetry estimates are wild guesses or show some geometric intuition. Teacher mentally flags 2–3 learners with interesting misconceptions to cold-call during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four for the Symmetry Safari. Each group receives: a set of pre-cut paper shapes (rectangle, square, equilateral triangle, circle, scalene triangle, regular hexagon), two leaves collected from the school compound, one Kanga fabric swatch (approx. 10 cm × 10 cm), one bottle cap, and one small acrylic plane mirror. Task 1 — Folding Test: Learners fold each shape and object to find all lines of symmetry, marking each fold line with a pencil. Task 2 — Mirror Test: Learners place the plane mirror along each proposed fold line to verify whether the reflected half matches the other half exactly. Task 3 — Recording: Groups complete a class results table (drawn in exercise books) with columns: Object/Shape | Predicted lines of symmetry | Lines found by folding | Lines confirmed by mirror. Groups also sketch the letter 'A' mirror test result observed at the front of the class and add it to their table. Total activity time: 12 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Distribute materials. Say: 'Your job is to be symmetry detectives. Use folding AND the mirror to find every line of symmetry in each object. Record everything in your table. You have 12 minutes — start now.' 2. At the 4-minute mark, circulate and prompt any group that is only folding and not using the mirror: 'Have you tried placing the mirror along that fold line? What do you notice when you do?' [WAIT 10 seconds for response before moving on.] 3. At the 8-minute mark, pose a challenge to groups that finish early: 'Can you find a shape with zero lines of symmetry? Can you find one with infinite lines of symmetry? Add those to your table.' 4. At the 12-minute mark, say: 'Pencils down. Each group, count the total number of different symmetry values you found across all shapes. We will share results now.' 5. Cold-call 4 groups to report one shape each. Ask: 'Group 3 — Fatuma, how many lines did the equilateral triangle have, and how did the mirror help you confirm that?' [WAIT 10 seconds.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) via guided inquiry. Learners begin with physical folding (concrete), move to mirror verification (representational — the mirror creates an image), and record in a symbolic table (abstract notation). Connecting the plane mirror directly to the fold line builds the geometric intuition that a line of symmetry IS a mirror line — a key conceptual bridge to all subsequent lessons on reflection.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe group tables during circulation: (a) Does the group correctly identify that a circle has infinite lines of symmetry? (b) Does the group distinguish between a square (4 lines) and a rectangle (2 lines)? (c) Does the group correctly record 0 lines for the scalene triangle? (d) Is the mirror being placed on the fold line correctly, or is it being held at random angles? These observations reveal whether learners understand that a line of symmetry must produce a perfect match — the core property of reflection.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups share results and the class builds a consensus table on the board. The teacher then connects findings back to the phenomenon: the letter 'A' and the Kanga swatch are revisited. Learners are guided to articulate a working definition of a line of symmetry in their own words, then refine it using the mathematical language introduced by the teacher. Learners individually write a definition in their exercise books and answer two consolidation questions: (1) 'A regular hexagon has ___ lines of symmetry. Draw them.' (2) 'The letter A has ___ line(s) of symmetry. The letter S has ___ line(s) of symmetry. Explain the difference.' Learners then return to their original predictions and annotate them: 'I was right / I need to revise this because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Build the consensus table on the board by cold-calling one reporter per group. After each group reports, ask the class: 'Does anyone want to challenge or add to that?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] 2. Point to the letter 'A' on the board. Say: 'Based on your safari, Juma — where is the line of symmetry of letter A, and what does that tell us about the mirror image we saw?' [WAIT 15 seconds. If no response, prompt: 'Think about where you would fold the letter A so both halves match perfectly.'] 3. Introduce the formal definition: 'A line of symmetry divides a figure into two congruent halves that are mirror images of each other. We also call it a mirror line.' Write this verbatim on the board. Say: 'Copy this definition and then write it again in your own words.' 4. Cold-call 3 learners to read their own-words definitions aloud. Affirm correct use of 'congruent', 'halves', and 'mirror image'. 5. Connect to phenomenon: 'So when Amara checked her uniform in the mirror this morning — which line of symmetry was the mirror acting as?' [WAIT 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.] 6. Pose the consolidation questions. Give 4 minutes of silent individual work. Cold-call 2 learners to explain question 2.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) discussion. Learners are asked to make a claim (e.g., 'A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry'), cite evidence from their folding/mirror activity, and provide geometric reasoning. This strategy develops mathematical communication and connects the hands-on observation to formal geometric language, directly building toward the properties of reflection that will be formalised in Lesson 2.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the 'I was right / I need to revise' annotation as an exit indicator. Specifically look for: (a) Whether learners now correctly identify 1 vertical line of symmetry for letter A (not 0, not 2). (b) Whether learners distinguish between a shape having a line of symmetry and 'looking nice' — evidence of conceptual rather than aesthetic understanding. (c) Whether at least 80% of learners can correctly state the number of lines for square, rectangle, equilateral triangle, and circle in the consensus table.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes (or tears a small piece of paper). On the first, they write one question the lesson has raised for them about mirrors, reflection, or symmetry. On the second, they write one thing they are now sure about. The teacher collects the 'question' notes and reads selected ones aloud before grouping them on the class Driving Question Board under three emerging clusters: 'About the IMAGE', 'About the DISTANCE', and 'About the FLIP/REVERSE'. Learners copy the three clusters and their own question into their exercise books as the start of their personal DQB tracker.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'You have 2 minutes. Write your most burning question on the first note — something about mirrors or reflection that you genuinely do not yet understand. On the second, write one thing you are now confident about after today's safari.' [WAIT 2 minutes — no talking.] 2. Collect question notes. Read 6–8 aloud without attribution. Say: 'Listen — do these questions sound familiar? Give a thumbs-up if you had a similar question.' 3. Model clustering on the DQB: 'Wanjiru asked: Why does the image appear the same distance behind the mirror as I am in front? That goes under DISTANCE. Otieno asked: Why is the letter A reversed left-right but not upside down? That goes under FLIP/REVERSE.' 4. Invite 2 learners to place remaining notes on the board. 5. Say: 'This board belongs to all of us. Every lesson in this unit, we will come back and answer some of these questions. By the end of the unit, every question on this board should have an answer.' 6. Point to the driving question: 'Why does a mirror show a perfect copy of the world — and where exactly does that copy live?' Write it at the top of the DQB. Say: 'That is the question we are all trying to answer together.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with clustered question sorting. This metacognitive strategy makes learner thinking visible, creates shared intellectual ownership of the unit, and allows the teacher to diagnose which conceptual gaps are most prevalent. Clustering questions into 'IMAGE', 'DISTANCE', and 'FLIP' categories foreshadows the three key properties of reflection (congruence, equidistance, perpendicular bisector) that form the mathematical core of this sub-strand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review the 'sure about' notes: Are learners expressing genuine conceptual understanding ('A square has 4 lines of symmetry because it can be folded in 4 ways that match perfectly') or surface-level recall ('We used mirrors')? Review question notes: Are learners asking mathematical questions ('How do we calculate where the image is?') or only perceptual ones ('Why does my face look different in a mirror?')? The ratio of mathematical to perceptual questions indicates readiness to move into the properties of reflection in Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners draw their Initial Reflection Model in their exercise books. The model has three components: (A) A diagram — learners draw a simple plane figure (e.g., the letter 'A' or a Kanga-inspired shape) next to a vertical mirror line and sketch what they currently believe the image looks like, labelling 'object', 'mirror line', and 'image'. (B) A rule statement — learners complete the sentence: 'I think the mirror line works by ___.' (C) A question flag — learners star the one thing in their diagram they are least confident about. The teacher emphasises: 'This is your starting model. It does not have to be correct — it has to be honest. We will revise it every lesson until it is perfect.'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Say: 'Close your eyes for 10 seconds and picture Amara standing in front of her mirror this morning. Picture the letter A next to the mirror at the front of this class. Now open your eyes and draw what you saw — but this time, add labels.' [WAIT 10 seconds with eyes closed.] 2. Give 4 minutes for individual model drawing. Circulate. Do not correct diagrams — only prompt: 'Have you labelled the mirror line?' / 'Where do you think the image is — in front of the mirror or behind it?' [WAIT 10 seconds after each prompt.] 3. Cold-call 2 learners to hold up their models and describe them in one sentence each. Do NOT evaluate correctness publicly. Say: 'These are two honest starting models. We will revisit them next lesson.' 4. Say: 'On the back of your model page, write today's date and the words: INITIAL MODEL — Lesson 1. Leave space below — that is where you will write REVISED MODEL after Lesson 2.' 5. Close the lesson by returning to the phenomenon: 'Amara is still puzzled. The driver on the matatu is still checking his mirrors. The letter A is still on that board. Next lesson, we will find the exact geometric rules that explain every single thing we saw today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Model construction using the Predict-Observe-Explain-Model (POEM) cycle. Creating an explicit, labelled diagram forces learners to commit a mental model to paper, making misconceptions visible and revisable. The 'question flag' (starring the least confident part) builds scientific and mathematical humility and creates a personal anchor for revision in subsequent lessons. This model will be iteratively updated across the unit, providing a cumulative record of conceptual growth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan models during circulation for three specific indicators: (a) Does the learner place the image behind the mirror (correct) or in front of it (misconception to address in Lesson 2)? (b) Does the learner draw the image the same size as the object, or larger/smaller (foreshadows understanding of congruence)? (c) Does the learner draw the image as laterally reversed (correct intuition from the letter A observation) or as an identical non-reversed copy? Document 3–4 models that show the most common misconception for targeted discussion in Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did the Symmetry Safari generate genuine curiosity, or did it feel procedural? If groups moved through the folding task without discussing, consider adding a 'justify your fold' requirement in future iterations. (2) How rich were the questions on the DQB? If most questions were perceptual ('Why does my face look different?') rather than mathematical ('How far behind the mirror is the image?'), consider seeding the DQB with one teacher-modelled mathematical question to raise the level of discourse. (3) Were learners able to distinguish between a square (4 lines) and a rectangle (2 lines)? This distinction is a known stumbling block — if more than 30% of groups recorded the wrong value for a rectangle, plan a brief 3-minute re-engagement at the start of Lesson 2 using a folded A4 sheet of paper (rectangular) to make the distinction concrete. (4) Did the Initial Model activity reveal the expected misconception that the image is in front of the mirror? If so, hold those 3–4 flagged models and use them (anonymously) as discussion anchors at the start of Lesson 2's Observe phase. (5) Was 40 minutes sufficient? The Observe Phase (Symmetry Safari) tends to run long if materials are not pre-cut. For future delivery, ensure all cut-outs are prepared before the lesson begins.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: A bold letter 'A' placed beside a plane mirror in the classroom produced a mirror image that appeared laterally reversed (flipped left-right). Leaves from the school compound, paper cut-outs of rectangles, squares, equilateral triangles, circles, and Kanga fabric swatches were folded and tested with a plane mirror. Different shapes yielded different numbers of lines of symmetry: circle (infinite), square (4), rectangle (2), equilateral triangle (3), scalene triangle (0).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A line of symmetry divides a plane figure into two congruent halves that are exact mirror images of each other. It is also called a mirror line. Shapes can have zero, one, more than one, or infinitely many lines of symmetry depending on their geometry. The fold test and the mirror test both confirm the same lines of symmetry, showing that folding and reflecting are geometrically equivalent operations.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The mirror line acts as the line of symmetry — it is the invisible geometric rule that governs where the mirror image appears. When the letter 'A' is placed beside a mirror, the vertical line of symmetry of the letter aligns with the mirror line, producing a reversed image that is congruent to the original. The 'flip' observed in Amara's bedroom mirror and in the matatu's rear-view mirror is a consequence of reflection across a mirror line, which reverses the figure laterally while preserving all distances and sizes. This is the foundational property that the rest of the unit will make precise and quantitative.

LESSONS.title: Mirror, Mirror on the Wall — Properties of Reflection on a Plane Surface

slo.purpose: To enable learners to discover and formalise the three geometric properties of reflection on a plane surface through hands-on measurement and peer discussion.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) the image distance from the mirror line equals the object distance; (ii) the line joining an object to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line; (iii) the image is congruent to the object.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) determine the properties of reflection using objects and their images; (b) draw an image given an object and a mirror line on a plane surface; (c) measure and verify perpendicularity and equal distances using a ruler and set square.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate the role of reflection in real-life situations and take responsibility for instruments used during construction activities.
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners identified lines of symmetry and posed questions about the mirror behaviour they observe daily — in the bedroom mirror, the matatu side mirrors, and the letter 'A' demonstration. Lesson 2 moves from noticing to measuring: learners stand at known distances from a plane mirror to feel the phenomenon, then use ruler, set square, and plain paper to locate image points precisely and extract the three governing properties. This evidence becomes the geometric foundation the class will rely on for all subsequent Cartesian-plane and real-life reflection tasks.
slo.safetyNotes: Handle plane mirrors carefully — edges may be sharp. Place mirrors flat on desks when not in use. Learners with photosensitive conditions should be seated away from direct reflected sunlight.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what will happen to their image distance when they step closer to or further from a plane mirror. They then gather evidence in two phases: (1) a physical mirror activity where they stand at measured distances and record observations, and (2) a paper-based construction activity using a ruler and set square to locate image points for objects placed at various distances from a drawn mirror line. From their measurements learners identify and formalise the three properties of reflection. They connect every finding back to the anchoring phenomenon — the bedroom mirror, matatu rear-view mirrors, and the letter 'A' — and update the Driving Question Board with new evidence. The lesson closes with a cumulative model sketch that annotates the three properties geometrically.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive a half-page prediction slip showing a top-view diagram of a girl (labelled 'Amina') standing 30 cm in front of a plane mirror. Three questions are printed: (i) If Amina moves to 60 cm from the mirror, where will her image appear — closer, the same distance behind, or further behind the mirror? Mark your prediction with an X. (ii) If she raises her RIGHT hand, which hand does the image raise? Draw an arrow. (iii) Write one sentence: what invisible rule do you think determines exactly where the image lands? Learners work individually and silently for 4 minutes, then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes. The teacher takes a quick show-of-hands poll for each option on question (i) and records the tally visibly on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — Lesson 2'.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute prediction slips face-down. Say: 'Before we touch any equipment today, I want to know what your brain already thinks. Turn over your slip — you have 4 minutes, working alone and in silence.' Set a visible timer. After 4 minutes: 'Turn to your shoulder partner. Compare your predictions. Do you agree? You have 2 minutes.' After partner talk, conduct the poll: 'Hands up if you predicted the image moves closer.' Tally. 'Hands up — same distance.' Tally. 'Further away.' Tally. Cold-call 2 learners from the largest group and 1 from a minority group: 'Baraka, tell us the reasoning behind your prediction.' WAIT 12 seconds. Record their reasoning verbatim in a second column beside the tally labelled 'Our Reasoning'. Say: 'We are going to put every one of these predictions to the test right now. Keep your slip — you will revisit it at the end of class.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Then-Investigate (Elicit Prior Knowledge): surfacing predictions before evidence gathering activates schema, creates cognitive dissonance when results differ, and gives learners a personal stake in the upcoming measurements. Recording reasoning publicly makes thinking visible and gives the teacher diagnostic information about misconceptions (e.g. 'the image gets smaller when you move away').
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans slips as learners write and notes: (a) what fraction predict 'same distance' (correct); (b) whether learners draw the correct hand being raised (common error: same hand). Misconceptions about image size changing with distance flag learners who may need targeted questioning during the observation phase. Tally on board becomes a running record the class will verify.

framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Physical Mirror Activity (10 min): Groups of four receive one plane mirror (≥ 20 cm tall), a 1-metre tape measure, and a recording table with columns: Object Distance from Mirror (cm) | Estimated Image Distance from Mirror (cm) | Same / Closer / Further. One learner stands at 20 cm, 40 cm, 60 cm, and 80 cm from the mirror (marked with masking-tape strips on the floor). A second learner peers into the mirror from the side at eye level and calls out where the image appears to be. The group records. Roles rotate so each learner stands in front of the mirror at least once. Learners note in the final column whether the image appears to be the same size each time. PART B — Paper Construction Activity (15 min): Each learner receives a sheet of plain A4 paper, a ruler, and a set square. They draw a vertical mirror line M down the centre. They place an object point P₁ at 3 cm to the left of M, P₂ at 5 cm to the left, P₃ at 7 cm to the left, and P₄ at 4 cm to the left but 3 cm higher. For each point they: (i) draw a perpendicular from the point to M; (ii) extend it an equal distance on the other side; (iii) mark the image point P₁', P₂', P₃', P₄'. They then connect P₁P₂P₃ to form a triangle and connect the corresponding image points to form the image triangle. Learners measure: object distance vs. image distance for each point; the angle between PP' line and M; and the sides of the object triangle vs. image triangle. They record all measurements in a table with columns: Point | Object Distance (cm) | Image Distance (cm) | Angle PP' makes with M (°) | Are they equal?
framework.teacherMoves: PART A — Before groups begin, hold up the mirror: 'This is the same type of mirror Amina uses in her bedroom and the same principle behind the matatu driver's rear-view mirror. We are going to measure what it actually does.' Assign roles aloud. Circulate; after 3 minutes prompt: 'Has anyone noticed a pattern yet? Don't announce it — write it in your table.' Cold-call one group at the 8-minute mark: 'Zawadi, what does your table show so far?' WAIT 10 seconds. Affirm data, not conclusions yet: 'Interesting data — hold your conclusion until Part B confirms it.' PART B — Model the first construction step on the board with an oversized compass and ruler: 'I draw a perpendicular from P₁ to M — that means a 90-degree angle, confirmed with the set square like this.' Demonstrate set-square placement. Then step back: 'Now you complete P₁ through P₄. I will circulate and ask you to show me your set square is flush against M.' Circulate and check every pair. At the 12-minute mark ask the class to freeze: 'Everyone measure the angle that the line P₁P₁-prime makes with M and write it. I am going to cold-call three people.' WAIT 12 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners across the room. Record responses on the board. Ask: 'What do all three answers have in common?' WAIT 10 seconds. Then: 'Now measure object distance vs. image distance for each point and compare the sides of your two triangles.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-Collection-and-Pattern-Detection (Structured Observation): the two-part sequence — physical mirror first, then precise paper construction — moves learners from qualitative noticing ('the image seems the same distance away') to quantitative confirmation (measured cm values). This mirrors the NGSS practice of Planning and Carrying Out Investigations. The structured recording table prevents premature closure and ensures every learner has personal data to reason from in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Set-square held correctly against M — teacher physically checks 100% of pairs during Part B. (2) Object distance and image distance columns show equal values (±1 mm tolerance acceptable) — if a learner's table shows discrepancies > 2 mm, teacher asks 'Did you extend the perpendicular exactly the same length on both sides? Show me how you measured.' (3) Angle column shows 90° — any value far from 90° indicates the perpendicular was not constructed correctly. (4) Triangle sides comparison shows equality — confirms congruence property.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners examine their completed tables from Part B and, working in pairs, draft three 'property statements' in their own words. After 5 minutes, the class participates in a Numbered-Heads-Together activity: each group of four numbers off 1–4. The teacher calls a number; that learner shares one property. The class evaluates each statement against their own data and refines the wording collaboratively until consensus is reached. The teacher scribes the agreed formal statements on the board: PROPERTY 1 — The image distance from the mirror line equals the object distance from the mirror line (object distance = image distance). PROPERTY 2 — The line joining any object point to its corresponding image point is perpendicular to the mirror line. PROPERTY 3 — The image is congruent to the object (same size and shape, laterally reversed). Learners copy the three formalised properties into their notebooks under the heading '2.2 Reflection — Properties'. They then apply the properties immediately to two quick exercises: (a) Given a mirror line and a point 4.5 cm from it, locate and label the image point; (b) Otieno stands 1.2 m from a plane mirror at Nairobi's Railways Museum hall of mirrors — how far is his image from the mirror, and what is the total distance between Otieno and his image?
framework.teacherMoves: After pairs draft their property statements: 'I want each pair to have three statements written. You have 5 minutes. Go.' WAIT — circulate silently reading drafts. After 5 minutes: 'Numbers-Heads-Together — number off in your group now: 1, 2, 3, 4.' Pause. 'All number-2s — stand up. Number-2 from Group A — Fatuma — read Property 1 as your group wrote it.' WAIT 12 seconds. Write Fatuma's words verbatim on the board. 'Class, look at your own data. Does Fatuma's statement match what you measured? Thumbs up, thumbs sideways, or thumbs down.' Address thumbs-sideways: 'Hamisi, what part doesn't match your data?' WAIT 10 seconds. Refine the statement live. Repeat for Properties 2 and 3 with number-3 and number-4 learners. Once all three are formalised, cold-call for the quick exercises: 'Exercise (b) — Otieno and the Railways Museum mirror. Who can set up the calculation? I need someone who hasn't spoken yet.' WAIT 12 seconds. 'Chebet — go ahead.' Confirm: image is 1.2 m behind mirror; total distance = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4 m. Explicitly connect: 'Now think back to Amina this morning. Her image in her bedroom mirror is the same distance behind the glass as she is in front. Which property explains that?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Numbered-Heads-Together with Collaborative Refinement (NGSS Constructing Explanations): by requiring learners to draft statements before hearing correct wording, this strategy ensures the formal properties emerge from their own data rather than from teacher transmission. The public refinement process models mathematical argumentation — a core mathematical process skill in the KICD curriculum — and gives every learner ownership of the final statements.
framework.formativeAssessment: During the Numbered-Heads-Together round, teacher listens for: (1) Use of the word 'perpendicular' — absence suggests the concept needs re-teaching; (2) Conflation of 'congruent' with 'identical' without noting lateral reversal — probe with 'Is the image exactly the same, or is anything different?'; (3) Correct calculation of 2.4 m total distance in the Otieno exercise — errors here often indicate learners added image distance to mirror thickness rather than to object distance. Quick written check: teacher asks every learner to write one sentence answering 'Which property explains why the letter A looks flipped in a mirror?' — collected as an exit ticket for this phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes — one green, one orange. On the GREEN note they write one thing they can now answer about the driving question ('Why does a mirror show a perfect copy of the world — and where exactly does that copy live?'). On the ORANGE note they write one new question that today's evidence raised but has not yet answered. Learners post their notes on the class DQB, which is divided into three columns: 'What We Predicted', 'What Evidence Showed', 'New Questions'. The teacher reads three orange notes aloud and the class votes (hands) on which question is most important to investigate next. The winning question is circled and dated as 'Most Urgent — Lesson 3 target'.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes. 'You have 3 minutes — GREEN: one thing our measurements today let you answer about the driving question. ORANGE: one new question our measurements raised. Write in full sentences.' After 3 minutes: 'Post green notes in the 'What Evidence Showed' column and orange notes in 'New Questions'.' Circulate to read notes as learners post. Select 3 orange notes that represent different kinds of questions (conceptual, procedural, application). Read each aloud: 'Kamau asks: Does this work the same way if the mirror line is slanted — like a tilted mirror in a barbershop?' Read a second. Read a third. 'Hands up for the question you most want answered in our next lesson.' Tally. Circle the winner. 'We will track this question all the way to Lesson 8. Write it in your notebook under our Driving Question.' Explicitly retrieve predictions from the slip: 'Look at your prediction slip. Put a tick next to each prediction today's evidence confirmed, and a cross next to each it disproved. You do not need to hand it in — it is your personal evidence record.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board — Evidence Mapping (NGSS Engaging in Argument from Evidence): the DQB makes the cumulative inquiry arc visible and habituates learners to distinguishing 'what we know from evidence' from 'what we still wonder'. The prediction-slip revisit creates a metacognitive moment — learners experience the productive discomfort of having predictions corrected by data, which deepens understanding more than being told the correct answer at the outset.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all green sticky notes after class to assess whether learners can articulate the three properties in their own words and connect them to the driving question. A green note that says only 'the image is behind the mirror' without reference to distance or perpendicularity signals incomplete understanding. Orange notes are analysed for scope: questions about curved mirrors, Cartesian-plane mirror lines, or lateral reversal indicate readiness for extension; questions about basic measurement procedure indicate learners who need consolidation before Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open to their cumulative model page (started in Lesson 1 with a sketch of Amina and her bedroom mirror). They add a top-view diagram of the bedroom scene labelled with: (i) a double-headed arrow between Amina and the mirror line annotated 'd_object'; (ii) a matching double-headed arrow on the image side annotated 'd_image = d_object'; (iii) a dashed line joining Amina to her image labelled '90°' where it crosses the mirror line; (iv) a small congruence symbol (≅) between Amina's figure and the image figure. In a text box beside the diagram they write: 'My model now explains: the image appears as far behind the mirror as I stand in front, because Property 1 says object distance = image distance. It is the same size because the image is congruent (Property 3). The image appears directly across the mirror because the joining line is perpendicular (Property 2).' Below this they write: 'My model cannot yet explain: [student fills in — e.g., what happens when the mirror line is tilted, or how to find the image on a coordinate grid].' The final 3 minutes are used for a partner gallery walk: partners swap model pages, read each other's annotations, and write one specific 'I notice…' comment on a sticky note attached to the page.
framework.teacherMoves: Project the Lesson 1 model sketch on the board (photograph taken at the end of Lesson 1). 'Here is where our model was at the end of last lesson — we knew mirrors existed and we had questions. Today we have evidence. Open your model page.' Walk through the labelling step by step: 'First, draw the double-headed arrow for object distance and label it d_object. I'll wait while you do that.' WAIT 20 seconds. 'Now mirror it on the image side, d_image, and write the equation. Set squares away — just annotate.' WAIT 20 seconds. 'Add the 90-degree label at the crossing point.' WAIT 15 seconds. 'Congruence symbol between Amina and her image.' WAIT 15 seconds. 'Now the text box — 3 sentences: what my model explains, which property it uses, what it still can't explain.' WAIT 3 minutes. Circulate and read text boxes; stamp or initial completed models. For the gallery walk: 'Swap pages with your partner. Read carefully. Write one 'I notice…' on their page — something specific about their diagram or explanation.' WAIT 2 minutes. 'Return pages.' Close: 'By Lesson 8 this model will be able to explain everything we see in Amina's mirror, in the matatu's mirrors, and in the letter-A demonstration. Today you added the three pillars. Hold on to this model — it grows with us.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (NGSS Developing and Using Models): requiring learners to annotate the same diagram across multiple lessons externalises the growth of their understanding and prevents fragmented knowledge. The 'what my model cannot yet explain' prompt is deliberate — it sustains productive epistemic humility and keeps the inquiry arc open, motivating subsequent lessons. The partner gallery walk introduces peer critique as a mathematical practice.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks model pages for three specific indicators: (1) Both distance arrows labelled and equation d_object = d_image written — if missing, learner did not internalise Property 1; (2) '90°' correctly placed at the intersection, not elsewhere on the diagram — misplacement indicates confusion between the perpendicular property and the mirror line itself; (3) Congruence symbol present and the text box explicitly names all three properties — absence of any property in the text box flags a gap. Models are photographed for the teacher's record and returned with a written question prompt tailored to each learner's identified gap, ready for the start of Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider the following questions: (1) During the Predict Phase, what was the most common misconception on prediction slips — did learners think the image size changes with distance? How will you address this in Lesson 3? (2) In Part B of the Observe Phase, were learners able to use the set square correctly to construct perpendiculars, or was the technique a barrier that slowed the investigation? If so, consider a 3-minute set-square drill at the start of Lesson 3. (3) Did the Numbers-Heads-Together produce all three properties, or did Property 2 (perpendicularity) consistently fail to emerge? If learners kept conflating 'opposite side' with 'perpendicular', plan a targeted re-teach using the analogy of the road crossing the river at right angles — a context familiar from Kenyan geography lessons. (4) Review all green sticky notes: what percentage articulated the connection between the measured data and the anchoring phenomenon (Amina's mirror, matatu mirrors, letter A)? If fewer than 70% made the connection explicitly, open Lesson 3 by cold-calling learners to make that connection before moving to Cartesian-plane reflection. (5) Which orange DQB question won the vote? Ensure your Lesson 3 plan directly addresses it in the opening Predict phase.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners stood at measured distances (20 cm, 40 cm, 60 cm, 80 cm) from a plane mirror and recorded the apparent position of their image. They then constructed image points for four object points on plain paper using a ruler and set square, measuring object distance, image distance, and the angle the joining line made with the mirror line for each point. They also compared the sides of an object triangle with those of its image triangle.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: From their measurements learners discovered and formalised three properties of reflection on a plane surface: (1) object distance from the mirror line equals image distance from the mirror line; (2) the line joining an object point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line; (3) the image is congruent to the object. They applied these to calculate Otieno's total distance from his image (2.4 m) in a Kenyan context and annotated Amina's bedroom mirror scenario with all three properties.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The three formalised properties explain why Amina's bedroom mirror shows her image the same distance behind the glass as she stands in front (Property 1), why the image appears directly 'across' the mirror rather than at an angle (Property 2), and why every detail — the Kanga pattern, the button count, the letter A — is preserved in size and shape even though it is laterally reversed (Property 3). The matatu driver's rear-view mirror follows the same three rules, so vehicles behind appear at a true proportional distance.

LESSONS.title: Drawing Images on a Plane Surface — Construction Practice

slo.purpose: To develop learners' ability to accurately construct reflected images of plane figures across horizontal, vertical, and oblique mirror lines using a geometrical set, and to annotate constructions with object distance, image distance, and perpendicular bisectors.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) the image of a point under reflection lies on the perpendicular from the point to the mirror line, at an equal distance on the opposite side; (ii) this rule holds for any orientation of the mirror line — horizontal, vertical, or oblique; (iii) the image of a plane figure is congruent to the object and laterally reversed.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) use a ruler and set square to drop a perpendicular from each vertex of a plane figure to the mirror line; (ii) measure and mark the image vertex at the same distance on the opposite side; (iii) join image vertices to construct the complete reflected figure; (iv) label object distance (d₀), image distance (dᵢ), and the perpendicular bisector for each corresponding pair of points.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate the precision and care required in geometric construction, recognising that the neat, rule-governed behaviour of mirror images — as seen in the morning bedroom mirror, the matatu side mirrors, and the teacher's letter 'A' demonstration — is a direct consequence of the exact geometric properties they are constructing by hand.
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1 and 2 learners identified lines of symmetry and discovered the properties of reflection (equal distances, perpendicularity, congruence, lateral reversal) through physical objects and plane mirrors. Lesson 3 now demands that learners operationalise those properties: using only a geometrical set, they must construct — not just observe — the precise location of a reflected image. This bridges observation and formal geometric reasoning, and directly answers a growing Driving Question Board question: 'What invisible rule governs exactly where the image lands?'
slo.safetyNotes: Compasses have sharp points — learners must keep compass points directed downward onto the paper and must not wave instruments. Rulers and set squares should be placed flat on desks when not in use. Learners working in pairs should agree on who holds the ruler before the other marks, to avoid slipping instruments.

LESSONS.overview: Learners use rulers, set squares, and compasses from their geometrical sets to construct reflected images of triangles, quadrilaterals, and an irregular polygon across three mirror-line orientations (horizontal, vertical, oblique). The teacher models each step with a think-aloud on the board, narrating every geometric decision. Learners then practise in pairs on plain paper, annotating each construction with object distance (d₀), image distance (dᵢ), and the perpendicular bisector of each corresponding pair of vertices. The lesson is anchored throughout in the phenomenon: each construction is framed as "building the invisible geometric rule that explains why Aisha's reflection in her bedroom mirror appears exactly as far behind the glass as she stands in front of it, and why the letter 'A' the teacher held up was the same size but perfectly flipped."

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive a plain-paper worksheet showing a scalene triangle ABC and a vertical mirror line m drawn 4 cm to its right. Without any instruments, they sketch — freehand — where they predict the reflected image A'B'C' will appear, and jot a one-sentence rule they are using to guide their sketch. They share predictions with a neighbour for 90 seconds.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute worksheets face-down. Say: 'Before we touch our geometrical sets today, I want to see what your brain already knows. Turn your sheet over — you have 90 seconds to sketch, freehand, where you think the mirror image of triangle ABC will appear across line m. Write one sentence explaining your rule. Go.' Set a visible timer for 90 seconds. Circulate silently — do NOT correct. After time, say: 'Turn to your neighbour. In 30 seconds, tell them one thing your sketches agree on and one thing that is different.' Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Kamau and Njeri — what did you agree on?' / 'Akinyi and Omondi — where did your images differ?' / 'Wanjiku and Mwangi — what rule did you both write down?' Allow 10 seconds of wait time after each question before accepting responses. Record 2–3 student-stated rules on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions'. Do not confirm or deny — say: 'Let's find out which of these rules survives today's constructions.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-Compare: by committing a freehand prediction to paper before instruction, learners activate and expose their current geometric mental models. The public posting of student-stated rules creates cognitive stakes — learners are motivated to test their own claim during construction.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans sketches during circulation for two observable indicators: (1) Has the learner placed the image on the correct side of the mirror line (opposite to the object)? (2) Does the image appear roughly the same size as the object? Learners who place the image on the same side, or dramatically resize it, are noted for targeted support during the Observe phase. Teacher does not intervene — data is for grouping decisions only.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher performs a slow, narrated step-by-step construction of the reflection of triangle ABC across the vertical mirror line on the board (large format, using a metre ruler and chalk set square). Learners watch and annotate a printed 'construction guide' card that lists each step as a blank to be completed. After the modelled triangle, the teacher constructs a second example — a rectangle across a horizontal mirror line — at increased pace, narrating less. Learners then open their geometrical sets and replicate both constructions on plain paper. They annotate: label each vertex pair (e.g. A → A'), draw and label the perpendicular from A to m, mark d₀ and dᵢ with a double-headed arrow, and highlight the perpendicular bisector. Finally, each learner attempts an oblique (45°) mirror line with an irregular quadrilateral — a shape chosen because it cannot be 'guessed' by symmetry intuition alone.
framework.teacherMoves: Stand at the board with a large-format version of the worksheet. Say: 'Watch every move I make — I am going to think out loud so you hear the geometry, not just see the pencil move.' Step 1 — say: 'I choose vertex A. I need a line from A that hits mirror line m at exactly 90 degrees. I place my set square with the right-angle corner on m and slide it until the vertical edge passes through A.' Draw the perpendicular. Step 2 — say: 'I measure the distance from A to m along this perpendicular — I get 3 cm. I mark a point A’ exactly 3 cm on the OTHER side of m, along the same perpendicular.' Mark A'. Step 3 — repeat for B and C. Step 4 — say: 'I join A’B’C’. I now label d₀ and dᵢ with arrows, and I mark the perpendicular bisector.' After completing triangle: pause and ask — 'Why must d₀ equal dᵢ? Think for 10 seconds.' [Wait 10 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Then say: 'Recall Aisha standing in front of her bedroom mirror this morning — she noticed her image appeared the same distance behind the glass as she stood in front. She just observed what you are now constructing.' Proceed to model the rectangle across the horizontal line at faster pace. Release to pair practice — circulate and ask targeted questions: 'Show me the perpendicular you dropped from this vertex.' / 'Is d₀ equal to dᵢ — measure and confirm.' / 'Your image vertex is 1 mm off — which step introduced the error?' For the oblique line task, say: 'The mirror line is now at 45° — your set square has a 45° angle. Which edge will you align to m to drop your perpendicular?' Wait 10 seconds before cold-calling.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelled Think-Aloud followed by Immediate Replication: the teacher narrates the geometric reasoning at each construction step (not just the procedure), so learners hear the 'why' (equal distances, perpendicularity) before they practise the 'how'. Immediate replication on plain paper consolidates procedural fluency while the reasoning is still audible in working memory. The deliberate progression — vertical, then horizontal, then oblique — builds generalisation: learners recognise that the same perpendicular-bisector rule governs all mirror-line orientations, just as the same geometry governs both Aisha's bedroom mirror and the matatu's angled side mirror.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher uses a 3-point circulating checklist per pair: (1) Perpendicular dropped correctly from each vertex to the mirror line — yes/no; (2) d₀ = dᵢ measured and confirmed — yes/no; (3) Image vertices joined to form a closed, congruent figure — yes/no. Any pair scoring 0–1 receives immediate side-by-side reteaching of Step 1. Any pair scoring 2 is prompted: 'Measure d₀ and dᵢ with your ruler — read the numbers aloud to each other.' Pairs scoring 3 proceed to the oblique challenge task.

framework.learnerExperience: Each pair receives a 'What went wrong?' card showing three common construction errors (image placed on same side as object; image vertex not at equal distance; lines joining image vertices not straight). Pairs identify which error matches a deliberately flawed construction printed on the card, write a one-sentence correction using geometric language (perpendicular, equidistant, bisector), and then revisit their own completed constructions to check for the same errors. The class reassembles for a whole-group discussion linking construction steps to the reflection properties stated in Lesson 2. Learners add a 'Construction Rule' box to their notes: 'For any point P at distance d from mirror line m, image P’ lies on the perpendicular from P to m, at distance d on the opposite side — so PP’ is bisected perpendicularly by m.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute 'What went wrong?' cards. Say: 'You have 3 minutes — identify the error on the card, write your correction sentence using at least two of these words: perpendicular, equidistant, bisector. Go.' Circulate. After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 pairs to read their correction sentence. After each, ask the class: 'Agree or refine? Thumbs up if you agree.' If thumbs are mixed, say: 'Omondi, what would you change in that sentence?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Then return to the board predictions posted in Phase 1. Say: 'Look at the rules we wrote at the start. Kwame wrote: "the image goes on the other side and is the same size." Is that now complete enough, or can we make it more precise?' Invite a volunteer to rewrite the rule using today's construction language. Anchor explicitly to phenomenon: 'When the maths teacher held up the letter A next to the plane mirror, the image A appeared perfectly preserved — same size, same shape. You have now constructed the geometric reason WHY. The perpendicular bisector property is the invisible rule Aisha and the class were puzzled by.' Dictate the Construction Rule box slowly for learners to copy.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Error Analysis (Worked Example Critique): presenting pre-made errors externalises common misconceptions without targeting any individual learner. Correcting a flawed example requires learners to articulate the correct property, which deepens understanding beyond procedural recall. Connecting the corrected rule back to the phenomenon ties formal geometric language to the original observable puzzle, advancing the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect correction sentences from three cold-called pairs. Observable indicator of understanding: the sentence must contain (i) a reference to perpendicularity, (ii) a statement of equal distances, and (iii) correct identification of which side the image appears on. Sentences that omit any of the three are flagged — the teacher notes those learners for re-engagement in Lesson 4's Cartesian-plane work.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes on a sticky note (or a paper strip if sticky notes are unavailable): one thing today's construction confirmed about the mirror phenomenon, and one new question it raised. They post contributions on the class Driving Question Board under two columns: 'We can now explain…' and 'We still wonder…'. The class does a 2-minute silent gallery walk of new postings, then the teacher reads two 'still wonder' questions aloud for the class to decide: 'Is this answered by what we already know, or does it need future investigation?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take a sticky note. On one side write: one thing today's construction proves about why Aisha's image is exactly as far behind her mirror as she stands in front. On the other side write: one question today raised that we haven't answered yet. You have 90 seconds.' Circulate — prompt stuck learners: 'Think about the oblique mirror line task — did anything surprise you?' After posting, read two 'still wonder' notes aloud — e.g. 'Does the rule still work if the mirror line is curved?' / 'What happens when two mirror lines cross?' Say to class: 'Hands up — answered already, or needs future lessons?' Tally publicly. Say: 'The question about what happens when the mirror line is on a coordinate grid — that is exactly where we go next.' Leave both columns visible for the remainder of the unit.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board — Progressive Disclosure: the DQB functions as a public, cumulative knowledge-tracking tool. Separating 'we can explain' from 'we still wonder' makes the boundary of current understanding visible to both learners and teacher. Learner-generated questions in the 'still wonder' column become the motivational bridge to Lesson 4 (reflection on a Cartesian plane), preserving the narrative of the phenomenon rather than treating lessons as isolated topics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all posted 'we can now explain' notes before the next lesson. Observable success indicator: the note references at least one of — perpendicular bisector, equal distances, or congruent image — in connection to the phenomenon (mirror / Aisha / letter A). Notes that are purely procedural ('we draw a perpendicular') without linking to the phenomenon indicate surface-level engagement and flag those learners for a targeted question at the start of Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative 'Reflection Model' — a large annotated diagram they began in Lesson 1 and updated in Lesson 2. Today they add a new panel labelled 'Lesson 3 — Construction Evidence'. In this panel they paste or redraw their best construction from today (the oblique mirror line with the irregular quadrilateral), annotate it fully (d₀, dᵢ, perpendicular bisector, vertex labels), and write two sentences: (1) what this construction proves about the location of the image, and (2) how this explains one specific detail from the morning phenomenon (Aisha's mirror, the matatu side mirror, or the letter A). Pairs share their two sentences with another pair and suggest one improvement to each other's wording.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Reflection Model from Lessons 1 and 2. You are adding today's construction evidence. Choose your clearest construction — the oblique mirror line — and paste or redraw it carefully in the new panel. Annotate completely: d₀, dᵢ, perpendicular bisector, all vertices. Then write your two sentences. You have 5 minutes.' Circulate and read sentences as they are written. Prompt with: 'Your first sentence says the image is the same distance away — can you add the word perpendicular to make that more precise?' / 'Your second sentence mentions Aisha — can you say exactly which property of your construction explains what she saw?' After 5 minutes: 'Share your two sentences with the pair next to you. Give them one improvement suggestion — something they could add or make more precise. 2 minutes.' Cold-call one pair to read their final second sentence to the class. Close with: 'Your model is growing. In Lesson 4 we move the mirror line onto a coordinate grid — and your model will need a new panel to show what changes and what stays exactly the same.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: the multi-lesson annotated diagram externalises learners' growing conceptual model of reflection, making prior knowledge visible and revisable. Requiring learners to connect the new construction panel explicitly to the phenomenon prevents the model from becoming a mere collection of diagrams — each addition must advance the explanation of the driving question. Peer sentence-sharing introduces low-stakes critique that sharpens geometric language use.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects models at the end of the lesson and checks two indicators before Lesson 4: (1) Is the oblique-mirror construction correctly annotated with d₀ = dᵢ confirmed and perpendicular bisectors drawn? (2) Do the two written sentences correctly link a geometric property (perpendicularity / equal distance / congruence) to a specific observable detail from the phenomenon? Models meeting both indicators are ready for the Cartesian-plane extension. Models meeting only one indicator receive a written prompt: 'Add the missing property — which measurement or line is not yet labelled?' Models meeting neither indicator trigger a brief one-to-one review at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Construction accuracy — what proportion of pairs correctly achieved d₀ = dᵢ and a properly dropped perpendicular on the oblique mirror line? If fewer than two-thirds succeeded, Lesson 4 should open with a 5-minute re-modelling of the oblique case before introducing the Cartesian grid. (2) Language precision — did learners use 'perpendicular bisector', 'equidistant', and 'congruent' spontaneously in the Explain phase, or only when prompted? If prompted, build a vocabulary warm-up into Lesson 4. (3) DQB quality — do the 'still wonder' questions show genuine curiosity about the Cartesian plane, or are they still at the level of 'why does the image flip?' (a Lesson 2 question)? If the latter, the phenomenon connection may need strengthening in the Lesson 4 hook. (4) Equity check — were the same 3–4 learners cold-called throughout? Review cold-call notes and ensure different learners are targeted in Lesson 4. (5) Time management — was there sufficient time for the full oblique-line construction, or was it rushed? If rushed, consider whether the 'What went wrong?' card in Phase 3 can be set as a homework task to recover time, given that plain-paper plain-language construction is the core Grade 10 KICD skill for this sub-strand.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners watched the teacher construct the reflected image of a triangle and a rectangle across vertical and horizontal mirror lines, narrating each geometric step (perpendicular from vertex to mirror line; measuring and marking equal distance on the opposite side; joining image vertices). They then observed their own constructions take shape on plain paper using rulers and set squares.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The image of any point P under reflection lies on the perpendicular from P to the mirror line m, at a distance equal to the distance from P to m — on the opposite side. This means m is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its image. This rule holds regardless of whether m is horizontal, vertical, or oblique, and explains precisely why Aisha's image appears exactly as far behind her bedroom mirror as she stands in front of it.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using the perpendicular-bisector construction rule, learners can now explain: (1) why the image is the same size as the object (congruence is preserved because every vertex is mapped by the same equal-distance rule); (2) why the image appears 'behind' the mirror at the same distance as the object is 'in front' (d₀ = dᵢ by construction); and (3) why the image is laterally reversed (the perpendicular mapping flips the left–right orientation). These three facts together answer the core puzzle of the phenomenon — the driving question 'where exactly does the copy live?' now has a geometric construction answer.
