LESSONS.title: Reflection on the Cartesian Plane I — Mirror Lines Along the Axes (x = 0 and y = 0)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: Cartesian plane reflection, x-axis mirror line, y-axis mirror line, coordinate rules reflection, image coordinates

slo.purpose: Learners move the mirror line from a physical surface onto a Cartesian grid and discover the exact coordinate transformation rules for reflection in the y-axis (x = 0) and the x-axis (y = 0), directly explaining why Aisha's image appears laterally reversed yet the same size and distance behind her mirror.
slo.knowledge:
• State the coordinate rule for reflection in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y)
• State the coordinate rule for reflection in the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y)
• Explain that the mirror line (x = 0 or y = 0) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each object point to its image point
slo.skills:
• Plot object vertices and their reflected images accurately on a Cartesian plane given the coordinate rules for x = 0 and y = 0
• Verify reflections by checking that the mirror line is equidistant from and perpendicular to each object–image pair
• Derive the coordinate rule by comparing object and image coordinates in a table
slo.attitudes:
• Demonstrate precision and care when plotting points and labelling coordinates on a Cartesian plane
• Appreciate that abstract coordinate rules are rooted in the same physical mirror properties encountered in everyday Kenyan life
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners established the three physical properties of reflection and practised constructing images on a plane surface. Lesson 4 relocates the mirror line onto the Cartesian plane: the y-axis becomes Aisha's bedroom wall mirror and the x-axis becomes the floor mirror in the matatu, letting learners derive precise algebraic rules that will power all subsequent coordinate-reflection work and ultimately answer why the image appears exactly as far behind the glass as the object is in front.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure sharp pencils are handled carefully during construction work. Rulers should be passed — not thrown — between partners.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson bridges the physical mirror work of Lessons 1–3 with the algebraic precision of coordinate geometry. Learners begin by predicting what happens to the coordinates of a point when it is reflected in a vertical or horizontal mirror, drawing on what they already know: the image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front. They then observe the pattern by plotting triangles and quadrilaterals that represent landmarks on a simplified grid map of a school compound in Nairobi, reflecting them in both axes, and recording a systematic table of object and image coordinates. The pattern in the table leads them to state the two coordinate rules explicitly.

In the Explain phase learners apply the rules to new shapes — including a quadrilateral whose vertices are labelled with distances matching the matatu rear-view mirror scenario from the anchoring phenomenon — and verify each image by the three properties established in Lesson 2 (equal distance, perpendicularity, congruence). The teacher guides learners to see that x = 0 is simply the y-axis acting as a mirror wall, and y = 0 is the x-axis acting as a mirror floor, so the algebraic rules are not arbitrary but follow inevitably from the geometry already understood.

By the end of the lesson learners can predict where any polygon's image will land under reflection in either axis without constructing perpendiculars — they simply apply (x, y) → (−x, y) or (x, y) → (x, −y). This quantitative power advances the driving question: the "invisible rule" governing where the image lands is now expressed as a coordinate transformation, and the reason the image is the same size but laterally flipped is encoded in the sign change on exactly one coordinate.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-sheet showing a Cartesian plane with a single triangle ABC plotted in Quadrant I (A = (2, 3), B = (5, 3), C = (5, 7)). Without any instruction, learners individually write down: (1) the coordinates they predict the image triangle A'B'C' will have after reflection in the y-axis (x = 0), and (2) the coordinates they predict after reflection in the x-axis (y = 0). They record their reasoning in one sentence next to each prediction. After 3 minutes learners share predictions with a partner and note any disagreements on a sticky note to post on the Driving Question Board.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the half-sheet and say: 'You have already built images with a ruler and set-square. Now the mirror is the y-axis — the vertical line down the middle of your grid. Without drawing anything yet, predict the coordinates of the image. Write your prediction and your reason. You have 3 minutes — work alone.' [Allow 3 minutes of silent individual thinking. Circulate and note 2–3 interesting or divergent predictions without correcting them.] After 3 minutes say: 'Compare with your partner. If you disagree, write your disagreement on the sticky note provided.' [Allow 1 minute for partner talk.] Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Pair at the front — what did you predict for A' when you reflect in the y-axis, and why?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each question before accepting a response.] Do NOT confirm or deny predictions. Say: 'Hold those ideas — we are about to gather evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict–Record–Compare: Learners commit written predictions to paper before observing, activating prior knowledge of the distance-and-perpendicularity properties from Lesson 2. Recording forces articulation of reasoning, not just a guess, and the partner comparison surfaces misconceptions (common prediction: image at (2, −3) instead of (−2, 3) for y-axis reflection) that the Observe phase will resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written predictions while circulating. Key indicator: does the learner apply 'same distance, opposite side' correctly to both coordinates or only to one? A learner who writes A' = (−2, 3) for y-axis reflection shows correct geometric intuition; a learner who writes (2, −3) is confusing the two axes. Teacher mentally flags these learners for targeted cold-calling during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs. Each pair receives a large-squared graph paper (or uses the ARES grid tool) showing a 'Nairobi School Grounds Grid Map' with four labelled buildings: the school gate at (1, 1), the science lab at (4, 1), the library at (4, 5), and the staffroom at (1, 5) — forming a rectangle GSLF. Learners are asked to: (1) plot and label the rectangle GSLF; (2) reflect it in the y-axis (x = 0) and plot the image G'S'L'F'; (3) reflect the original in the x-axis (y = 0) and plot image G''S''L''F''; (4) complete a three-column coordinate table (Object | Image in x=0 | Image in y=0) for all four vertices. They then look for the pattern and write a generalisation in words before converting it to algebraic notation.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the graph paper and say: 'This grid represents part of the grounds of a school in Nairobi — the y-axis is the school's main wall and the x-axis is the school fence. Plot the four buildings, then use everything you learnt in Lesson 2 — perpendiculars, equal distances — to reflect the rectangle in each axis. Fill in the table as you go. You have 10 minutes.' [Circulate. After 5 minutes, pause the class for 30 seconds: 'Stop and look at your table so far. What is happening to the x-coordinate when you reflect in the y-axis? What is happening to the y-coordinate?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds.] Cold-call 2 pairs to share partial observations. Then say: 'Continue — finish the table and write your generalisation.' After 10 minutes total, bring the class together. Ask: 'Who can tell me the pattern in one sentence — what changes and what stays the same?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Cold-call 3 individuals. Write their exact words on the board without editing, then ask: 'Can we write that using algebra? What would (x, y) become?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Table Pattern Recognition: By recording object and image coordinates in a structured three-column table — a classic science-and-engineering practice of analysing data — learners see the numerical pattern emerge across four data points simultaneously. The Nairobi school-grounds context anchors the abstract coordinates in a familiar spatial layout, making the sign-change rule feel geometrically motivated rather than arbitrary.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks tables for accuracy of all 8 image coordinates (4 per axis). Correct entries: reflection in x=0 gives G'=(−1,1), S'=(−4,1), L'=(−4,5), F'=(−1,5); reflection in y=0 gives G''=(1,−1), S''=(4,−1), L''=(4,−5), F''=(1,−5). Learners who swap sign changes (e.g., applying x-axis rule to y-axis reflection) need immediate pair-level intervention. Teacher also checks that generalisations are written before algebra is attempted — a learner who jumps straight to (−x, y) without a verbal statement has not yet consolidated the geometric meaning.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners apply the two coordinate rules to a new challenge: a triangle PQR representing the matatu from the phenomenon (P = (3, 2), Q = (6, 2), R = (6, 6)) is reflected in the y-axis to model the view in the driver's side mirror (the mirror wall = y-axis), and then the same triangle is reflected in the x-axis to model the rear-view mirror view (mirror floor = x-axis). Learners write the image coordinates using the rules — no construction required — and then verify one image by checking perpendicularity and equal distance for vertex P only (using the Lesson 2 method). Finally, learners write a concise two-sentence explanation connecting the sign-change rule back to Aisha's bedroom mirror: why does her image raise the opposite hand?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You now have the rules. Use them — no ruler, no perpendiculars — just the algebra — to write down the image of triangle PQR under reflection in x = 0 and then in y = 0.' [Allow 4 minutes.] After learners have written image coordinates, say: 'Now verify your answer for vertex P only using the perpendicular-and-equal-distance method from Lesson 2. This check tells us the rule is consistent with the geometry.' [Allow 3 minutes.] Cold-call 1 learner: 'Read me your image coordinates for the y-axis reflection.' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] Write them on the board. Ask the class: 'Thumbs up if you agree, thumbs to the side if you are unsure.' Address any thumbs-to-the-side directly. Then ask: 'Here is the big question — look at your image of P under x = 0. The x-coordinate changed sign. In Aisha's bedroom, she raises her right hand and the image raises what appears to be a left hand. Which coordinate is responsible for that flip, and why?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Conclude by writing on the board: 'Reflection in x = 0: (x, y) → (−x, y) — the horizontal distance flips, the vertical stays. Reflection in y = 0: (x, y) → (x, −y) — the vertical distance flips, the horizontal stays.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Rule–Verify–Connect: Learners first apply the algebraic rule (efficiency), then verify it geometrically (validity), then connect it to the anchoring phenomenon (meaning). This three-step sequence, adapted from the NGSS practice of using mathematics and computational thinking alongside constructing explanations, ensures the rule is not memorised in isolation but understood as an inevitable consequence of the geometry of mirrors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher looks for three things: (1) Correct image coordinates for PQR under both axes — P'=(−3,2), Q'=(−6,2), R'=(−6,6) for x=0; P''=(3,−2), Q''=(6,−2), R''=(6,−6) for y=0. (2) A valid perpendicularity check for vertex P showing PP' is horizontal (same y, opposite x) and midpoint of PP' lies on x=0. (3) The written explanation must explicitly name 'the x-coordinate changes sign' as the cause of the lateral flip. A vague answer ('the image is reversed') is flagged for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their sticky notes from the Predict phase. Each pair now writes two new sticky notes: one labelled 'NOW I KNOW' stating the coordinate rule they have confirmed, and one labelled 'STILL WONDERING' raising a new question sparked by today's work (e.g., 'What happens if the mirror line is y = x instead of an axis?' or 'Can you reflect in a line that is not through the origin?'). Pairs post both notes on the class DQB under the columns 'Evidence Gathered — Lesson 4' and 'New Questions'. The class does a 2-minute silent gallery walk of the 'STILL WONDERING' notes.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'Our driving question asks where exactly the copy in the mirror lives. Today we found a coordinate address for it. Write on your green sticky note exactly what you now know about that address — use the algebraic rule. On your orange sticky note, write one question that today's lesson opened up that we have not yet answered.' [Allow 2 minutes for writing.] As pairs post notes, read two 'STILL WONDERING' notes aloud without attributing them: 'Someone is asking — what if the mirror line is diagonal? Another person asks — does the rule change if the shape is in Quadrant III? These are excellent questions. Our storyline will visit them.' Point to the DQB column for Lesson 5 and say: 'We will come back to those in our next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Know–Wonder Board Progression: The DQB is a cumulative public record of the class's growing understanding across all 8 lessons. By explicitly distinguishing 'NOW I KNOW' (evidence-based claims) from 'STILL WONDERING' (productive questions), learners practise the scientific practice of distinguishing what is established from what remains open — directly mirroring how mathematicians build theory incrementally.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all 'NOW I KNOW' sticky notes during the gallery walk. A correct entry names the rule symbolically, e.g., '(x, y) → (−x, y) for x = 0'. An incomplete entry such as 'the coordinates change' indicates the learner has not consolidated the rule and needs a follow-up question in the next lesson's warm-up. Teacher photographs the DQB state for the lesson record.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative unit model — a labelled diagram of Aisha's bedroom scenario that has been updated in each lesson. Today they add a Cartesian overlay: they sketch a small coordinate grid on their model, place Aisha at point (3, 0) and the mirror wall along the y-axis (x = 0), then write her image's coordinates as (−3, 0) and annotate: 'Rule: (x, y) → (−x, y). The mirror at x = 0 flips the x-coordinate, which is why Aisha's image raises the opposite hand — the left–right direction is the x-direction.' Learners also add an arrow labelled '2 × 3 = 6 m total distance' to connect to the Lesson 2 calculation. Finally, learners write one sentence at the bottom of their model updating their best current answer to the driving question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Update your model. Add the coordinate grid, place Aisha and her image, write the rule, and annotate why the hand appears to flip. You have 4 minutes.' [Circulate. Look specifically for whether learners place the mirror on x = 0 rather than between two grid lines, and whether the annotation explains the sign change geometrically.] After 4 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to read their driving-question update sentence aloud. [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds before accepting.] Affirm precision: 'I hear you saying the image lives at (−3, 0) because the rule flips the sign of x. That is the most precise answer we have given to our driving question so far — the copy lives at a coordinate address that is the mirror image of the object's address.' Say: 'In Lesson 5 we will move the mirror to the line y = x and see if our model needs updating again.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: The model is not redrawn each lesson but annotated and extended, making conceptual growth visible. Adding a coordinate overlay to the existing physical diagram makes explicit the connection between the geometric construction method (Lessons 2–3) and the algebraic rule (Lesson 4), embodying the NGSS practice of developing and using models as explanatory tools that evolve with evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks three elements in each learner's model: (1) Mirror line correctly drawn as the y-axis (x = 0), not as a freehand vertical line. (2) Aisha's image coordinates correctly stated as (−3, 0). (3) The annotation explicitly links the sign change in x to the lateral flip observed in the phenomenon. A model that shows correct coordinates but no explanatory annotation is rated 'Approaches Expectations' and earns a written prompt: 'Why does the x-coordinate change sign? What does that mean for Aisha's hand?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Observe phase, did learners complete the coordinate table with sufficient accuracy to see the sign-change pattern independently, or did most pairs need a hint? If hints were needed, consider pre-teaching the table structure as a warm-up in the next lesson.
2. Were learners able to articulate the difference between reflection in x = 0 (sign of x changes) and reflection in y = 0 (sign of y changes), or did a significant number confuse the two? Prepare a targeted 5-minute warm-up for Lesson 5 if more than one-third of the class conflated them.
3. Did the Nairobi school-grounds context make the coordinate work feel grounded and meaningful, or did learners treat it as a superficial label? Note any moments where a learner spontaneously connected the grid to a real spatial layout — these indicate the context is working.
4. How precise were learners' 'NOW I KNOW' sticky notes? Did most write the algebraic rule (x, y) → (−x, y), or only a verbal description? The level of symbolic precision on the DQB tells you whether the class is ready for the more abstract y = x mirror line in Lesson 5.
5. Did any learner's driving-question update sentence advance beyond 'the copy lives at (−x, y)' to include an explanation of why (because the mirror is perpendicular to the x-direction and equidistant)? If so, use that sentence as the opening provocation for Lesson 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: When triangle and rectangle vertices in Quadrant I were reflected in the y-axis (x = 0), only the x-coordinate changed sign while y stayed the same; when reflected in the x-axis (y = 0), only the y-coordinate changed sign while x stayed the same — confirmed across all eight vertices of the Nairobi school-grounds rectangle.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Reflection in the y-axis follows the rule (x, y) → (−x, y); reflection in the x-axis follows the rule (x, y) → (x, −y). In both cases the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each object point to its image, consistent with the three properties established in Lesson 2.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The coordinate rules explain precisely why Aisha's image appears laterally reversed: standing at x = 3 in front of her mirror wall (the y-axis, x = 0), her image is located at x = −3, so the left–right (x) direction is flipped while the up–down (y) direction is preserved — which is exactly why the image raises the opposite hand. The 'invisible rule' governing where the image lands is now a coordinate transformation.

LESSONS.title: Reflection on the Cartesian Plane II — The y = x Mirror Line

slo.purpose: Learners investigate reflection in the line y = x on the Cartesian plane, deduce the coordinate transformation rule (x, y) → (y, x), and consolidate all three Cartesian mirror lines (x = 0, y = 0, y = x) into a unified reference framework.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that reflection in the line y = x maps every point (x, y) to the image point (y, x); that the mirror line y = x is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each object point to its image; and that the three Cartesian mirror lines x = 0, y = 0, and y = x each produce a distinct, rule-governed coordinate transformation.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: plot object points and their images under reflection in y = x; state and apply the rule (x, y) → (y, x); draw the mirror line y = x; verify reflection properties (equal distance, perpendicularity) for the new mirror line; and select and apply the correct transformation rule when given a mixed set of Cartesian reflection problems.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that every mirror line — whether physical (the bedroom mirror, the matatu rear-view mirror) or abstract (a line on the Cartesian plane) — imposes a precise, predictable rule on where an image lands, building confidence in using mathematics to explain everyday observations.
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 3 and 4 learners discovered that the y-axis (x = 0) and x-axis (y = 0) mirror lines swap the sign of one coordinate, just as a physical mirror swaps left and right or near and far. Lesson 5 introduces a diagonal mirror — the line y = x — and shows that this line swaps the two coordinates entirely, (x, y) → (y, x). This mirrors the anchoring phenomenon: when Amina tilts the full-length mirror on her bedroom wall at 45°, her reflection is transformed in a completely new way. By comparing all three mirror lines in a summary table, learners build a complete geometric 'rule book' for plane reflection and move significantly closer to answering the driving question about where exactly the mirror-image copy lives.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Remind learners to handle rulers and geometrical set instruments with care. If graph paper is distributed as printed sheets, ensure scissors or sharp objects are not needed for this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: In this 40-minute lesson learners first predict what happens to coordinates when a point is reflected in the diagonal line y = x, using their knowledge of the bedroom mirror tilted at 45°. They then gather evidence by plotting three object points and their reflections on squared/graph paper (or a shared Cartesian grid on the board), measuring distances, and tabulating results. Through guided sensemaking they induce the rule (x, y) → (y, x), verify it geometrically, and consolidate it alongside the x = 0 and y = 0 rules in a three-row summary table. A mixed-problem practice set and a DQB update close the lesson. Throughout, the anchoring phenomenon — Amina's mirror, the matatu side mirrors, and the letter 'A' experiment — is explicitly revisited to ground every abstract rule in observable reality.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchoring phenomenon: Amina's mathematics teacher held a bold letter 'A' beside a plane mirror and the class saw a laterally reversed image. The teacher now poses a new scenario: 'Imagine Amina tilts that same mirror so it sits exactly along the diagonal line y = x on a Cartesian grid — at 45° to both axes. She places a point at (2, 5). Where do you predict the image will land?' Learners write their individual prediction (coordinate pair) in their exercise books, then share with a shoulder partner. Selected pairs are cold-called to share predictions with the class (teacher cold-calls 4 pairs). Predictions are displayed on a class 'Prediction Wall' (a section of the board left blank for this purpose) without judgment.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Display the anchoring phenomenon recap (30 seconds): 'In our last two lessons we found rules for the x-axis and y-axis mirror lines. Today we add a new mirror line — the diagonal y = x — just like tilting Amina's bedroom mirror at 45°.' 2. Draw a clear Cartesian grid on the board with the line y = x drawn in a contrasting colour. Mark point A(2, 5) visibly. 3. Pose the prediction prompt verbatim: 'Write down the coordinates you predict for the image of point A(2, 5) when it is reflected in the line y = x. You have 60 seconds — work silently and independently.' 4. Allow 60 seconds silent individual thinking. 5. 'Now turn to your neighbour and compare your predictions. Agree on ONE coordinate pair between you. 30 seconds.' 6. WAIT TIME: After calling 'ready', wait 10 seconds before cold-calling. 7. Cold-call exactly 4 pairs by name: 'Kariuki and Njeri — what did you predict?', 'Otieno and Akinyi?', 'Wanjiru and Mwangi?', 'Fatuma and Hassan?' 8. Record all four predictions on the Prediction Wall without commenting on correctness. 9. Ask: 'What pattern, if any, do you notice in your classmates' predictions?' Wait 10 seconds, take 2 volunteer responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-record prediction: By committing to a coordinate pair before instruction, every learner activates prior knowledge of the x = 0 and y = 0 rules and forms a personal hypothesis. Recording predictions publicly creates cognitive dissonance that the Observe phase will resolve, deepening retention of the correct rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has written a coordinate pair in their book within 60 seconds. Teacher scans the room during the silent minute to check participation. The spread of predictions on the Prediction Wall (e.g., whether learners offer (5, 2), (−2, −5), (−5, −2), or random guesses) reveals existing misconceptions about diagonal reflections that the teacher notes for targeted follow-up during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive (or open to) a pre-drawn Cartesian grid (x and y from −6 to 6) with the line y = x already drawn. Working in pairs, they complete a structured evidence-gathering table: they plot three object points — A(2, 5), B(−1, 3), C(4, −2) — then use a ruler to draw the perpendicular from each point to the line y = x, extend it an equal distance on the other side, and mark the image points A', B', C'. They measure and record: (i) the object coordinates, (ii) the image coordinates they find by construction, (iii) the perpendicular distance from object to mirror line, and (iv) the perpendicular distance from image to mirror line. They record all findings in a four-column evidence table in their books.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Distribute grids (or direct learners to draw on graph paper). Confirm the line y = x is visible: 'The line y = x passes through the origin at 45°. Check: does your line pass through (1,1), (2,2), (3,3)? Give me a thumbs-up when you can see that.' 2. Model the construction for point A(2, 5) live on the board: draw the perpendicular from A to the line y = x (remind learners how to use a set-square for perpendicularity), measure the distance, mark the image A' on the other side at the same distance. Narrate aloud: 'I am measuring exactly 2.1 cm from A to the mirror line; I mark 2.1 cm on the other side — this is A'.' 3. Say verbatim: 'Now you do points B and C with your partner. Use your ruler carefully. You have 8 minutes.' 4. Circulate; crouch to pair level; ask probing questions: 'How do you know your perpendicular is truly at 90° to y = x?', 'Is the image closer to or further from the line than the object?' 5. After 8 minutes: 'Pause. Read off the coordinates of A', B', C' from your grid and fill in the evidence table. You have 2 minutes.' 6. WAIT TIME before whole-class share: 10 seconds of silence after saying 'Pens down.' 7. Cold-call 3 individual learners (not pairs this time) to read their image coordinates aloud: 'Chebet, what are the coordinates of A'?', 'Mwenda, what did you get for B'?', 'Adhiambo, and C'?' Record responses on the board in a class evidence table next to the objects.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data-collection table: Requiring learners to record both the coordinate evidence AND the distance measurements simultaneously connects the algebraic rule to its geometric justification. The distance measurements directly mirror the anchoring phenomenon observation that 'the image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front' — now verified quantitatively on the Cartesian grid.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learner evidence tables should show A'(5, 2), B'(3, −1), C'(−2, 4) with equal perpendicular distances (to within ±0.2 cm measurement tolerance). Teacher checks at least 6 pairs' tables during circulation. Pairs whose image coordinates are not the correct swap are flagged — the teacher asks 'Can you count grid squares from your point to the mirror line and back?' to redirect without giving the answer.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher guides the class to extract the pattern from their evidence table. Learners compare object and image coordinate pairs, state the rule in words, write it in algebraic notation, and verify it against their Prediction Wall entries. They then complete a three-row Reflection Rules Summary Table comparing all three mirror lines studied. Finally, they apply the three rules to a set of four mixed practice problems, self-marking against answers revealed by the teacher.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Point to the class evidence table on the board: A(2,5)→A'(5,2); B(−1,3)→B'(3,−1); C(4,−2)→C'(−2,4). Ask verbatim: 'Look carefully at the object coordinates and the image coordinates. What do you notice? Write one sentence in your book. 30 seconds.' WAIT 10 seconds after pens go down before taking responses. Cold-call 4 learners. Steer toward: 'The x and y coordinates swap places.' 2. Ask: 'How do we write this as a mathematical rule? Try writing it using (x, y) → (?, ?).' Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners. Confirm and write prominently on the board: RULE: Reflection in y = x maps (x, y) → (y, x). 3. Return to the Prediction Wall: 'Which pairs predicted (5, 2) for A(2,5)? Stand up.' Celebrate correct predictors. Ask one incorrect predictor: 'What did you predict, and why do you think the rule is (y, x) rather than your answer?' (No judgment; frame as 'our prediction helped us notice the pattern.') 4. Distribute or display the three-row Reflection Rules Summary Table: headers — Mirror Line | Rule | Example. Learners fill in all three rows: x=0: (x,y)→(−x,y); y=0: (x,y)→(x,−y); y=x: (x,y)→(y,x). Give 3 minutes. 5. Phenomenon link — say verbatim: 'Think back to Amina's matatu ride. The side mirror showed vehicles behind her. If the road is like the x-axis and the mirror is the y-axis, the car at position (3, 1) appears at (−3, 1). But if Amina tilted that mirror to 45°, the car would appear at (1, 3). Different mirror angle — different rule — but always precise and predictable. That is what mathematics gives us.' 6. Mixed practice: display 4 problems (2 minutes each, individual silent work): (a) Reflect P(3,1) in y=x; (b) Reflect Q(−2,4) in x=0; (c) Reflect R(0,5) in y=0; (d) Reflect S(−3,−1) in y=x. After 8 minutes, reveal answers; learners self-mark. 7. Ask: 'Raise your hand if you got all four correct.' Then: 'Raise your hand if you got three.' Use this as a live participation check.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern-induction followed by rule consolidation in a comparison table: Learners first discover the y = x rule from their own data (inductive reasoning), then slot it into a growing framework alongside x = 0 and y = 0. The comparison table is a Knowledge Organiser — a single visual that encodes all three rules and allows learners to self-quiz. The mixed practice immediately transfers the rules to varied contexts, embedding procedural fluency alongside conceptual understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) All learners can write (x,y)→(y,x) correctly in their books — teacher checks 8 books during the table-filling activity. (ii) In mixed practice, the teacher notes which problem type produces the most errors (commonly Q(b) or Q(c) — sign errors on axes) and names the misconception aloud: 'I notice some learners changed BOTH coordinates for the x-axis reflection — remember, only the x-coordinate changes sign for x = 0.' (iii) The show-of-hands score on 4/4 versus 3/4 gives a rapid class-level accuracy read.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes one new understanding on a green sticky note and one remaining question on a yellow sticky note, then physically adds them to the class DQB. The teacher reads selected notes aloud and explicitly links the lesson's findings back to the driving question: 'Why does a mirror show a perfect copy of the world — and where exactly does that copy live?'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Hand out one green and one yellow sticky note per learner (or instruct learners to tear a page into two coloured-pencil-outlined boxes if physical notes are unavailable). 2. Say verbatim: 'On the GREEN note write: ONE thing you now know about where the image lives — be specific, use coordinates or the rule. On the YELLOW note write: ONE question you still have about reflections or mirror lines.' Allow 2 minutes silent writing. 3. Learners bring notes to the DQB (a section of the wall or a large piece of manila paper). Organise notes into two columns: WHAT WE NOW KNOW | WHAT WE STILL WONDER. 4. Teacher reads 3 green notes aloud, e.g., 'Waweru writes: The image in y=x is found by swapping the coordinates — (x,y) goes to (y,x).' Then reads 2 yellow notes, e.g., 'Akinyi asks: What happens if the mirror line is y = 2x instead of y = x?' 5. Explicitly connect to driving question — say verbatim: 'Our driving question asks WHERE EXACTLY the copy lives. After five lessons, we now have three precise mathematical addresses for images in Cartesian mirrors — and we have verified them with rulers and coordinates. Akinyi's question — y = 2x — is a preview of what more advanced mathematics can answer. Keep that question on the board.' 6. Point to the DQB and note the growing cluster of 'WHAT WE NOW KNOW' notes: 'Compare this column to where it was in Lesson 1. We are building a complete answer to our driving question, one mirror line at a time.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Metacognitive DQB curation: The two-colour sticky-note protocol separates consolidated knowledge (green) from productive uncertainty (yellow), making the boundary of understanding visible to both teacher and learner. Publicly reading selected notes validates diverse contributions and models scientific discourse — the practice of distinguishing evidence-based claims from open questions, directly paralleling the NGSS practice of 'Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Green notes should include at least one of: the rule (x,y)→(y,x), a reference to equal distances, or a mention of the mirror line y=x. A green note that only says 'reflection swaps things' signals surface-level understanding — the teacher notes that learner for follow-up in Lesson 6. Yellow notes that reference new mirror lines (e.g., y=−x, y=2) indicate readiness for extension and inform Lesson 6 planning.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve the cumulative geometric model they have been building since Lesson 1 (a Cartesian plane diagram showing object, image, and mirror line). They add the y = x mirror line in a new colour and annotate it with: (i) the algebraic rule (x,y)→(y,x), (ii) a plotted example showing A(2,5) and A'(5,2) with the perpendicular bisector drawn, and (iii) a one-sentence explanation of how this new mirror line changes the image compared to the x-axis and y-axis mirror lines. Learners who finish early are invited to also sketch what happens to a small triangle (with vertices at (1,2), (3,2), (3,4)) reflected in y=x, labelling all image vertices.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Say: 'Take out your cumulative reflection model. Today we add the third and most powerful mirror line we have studied.' Allow 30 seconds for learners to locate their models. 2. Demonstrate on the board: draw the line y=x in orange (or any new colour) on the existing model, plot A(2,5), draw the perpendicular to y=x, mark A'(5,2), and write the rule beside the mirror line. Talk aloud: 'I am adding y=x in orange so I can immediately see all three mirror lines at a glance — blue for x=0, red for y=0, orange for y=x.' 3. Learners work independently for 5 minutes to update their own model. Teacher circulates and checks: (a) Is the line y=x correctly drawn at 45° through the origin? (b) Is the example point and its image correctly placed? (c) Is the rule written accurately? 4. For the one-sentence comparison, prompt with: 'How is the y=x image different from the x=0 image of the same point? Think about A(2,5): where does it go for each mirror line?' WAIT 10 seconds. Take 2 volunteer responses before learners write. 5. With 2 minutes remaining, close by saying verbatim: 'Your model now holds three reflection rules. In our next lesson we will use this model to find the mirror line when we are only given the object and its image — working backwards, just like a detective. Keep your model safe.' 6. Extension task (stated aloud for fast finishers): 'Reflect the triangle with vertices K(1,2), L(3,2), M(3,4) in the line y=x. Label all image vertices and check that the image triangle is congruent to the original.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative annotated model revision: Each lesson learners physically add one new element to a single evolving diagram. This models the scientific practice of 'Developing and Using Models' — the model is never 'finished' but is refined with each new piece of evidence. The colour-coding (a different colour for each mirror line) creates a visual knowledge organiser that makes the three rules simultaneously comparable and aids long-term retrieval. The one-sentence comparison forces learners to articulate the conceptual difference between rules, not just apply them procedurally.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Teacher checks that the line y=x passes through (0,0), (1,1), (2,2) — a common error is drawing it through (0,1). The example point A' must be at (5,2), not (−2,−5) or another confusion. The one-sentence comparison should explicitly mention that x=0 negates the x-coordinate while y=x swaps both coordinates — a surface-level answer ('they are all reflections') prompts the teacher to ask: 'Show me numerically, using A(2,5) as your example, what is different.' The extension triangle task is collected from fast finishers and used as a stretch indicator for Lesson 6 grouping.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did learners successfully induce the rule (x,y)→(y,x) from their own plotted data, or did most need the teacher to tell them the rule directly? If the latter, consider providing a more scaffolded evidence table in Lesson 6 that explicitly asks 'What do you notice about the x-value of the object versus the y-value of the image?' (2) Which of the three Cartesian mirror lines caused the most confusion in the mixed practice? Plan a 5-minute warm-up at the start of Lesson 6 targeting that specific rule. (3) Were all learners able to draw the line y=x correctly at 45° through the origin? If not, a brief graphing-skills mini-lesson may be needed before Lesson 6's 'finding the mirror line' work. (4) Did the DQB yellow notes reveal any profound questions (e.g., about non-standard mirror lines such as y=−x) that could enrich Lesson 6 or be set as a bonus investigation for high-readiness learners? (5) Was 40 minutes sufficient for the model-building update, or did the Explain phase's mixed practice overrun? Adjust timing by reducing mixed-practice problems from 4 to 3 if needed.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners plotted three object points (A(2,5), B(−1,3), C(4,−2)) on a Cartesian grid and used a ruler to construct their reflections in the line y = x, recording both the image coordinates and the perpendicular distances from each point to the mirror line.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners induced and stated the rule that reflection in the line y = x maps every point (x, y) to the image point (y, x) — the two coordinates swap; they verified that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining object to image; and they completed a three-row summary table comparing the transformation rules for all three Cartesian mirror lines studied (x = 0, y = 0, y = x).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained that a diagonal mirror at 45° (the line y = x) swaps the two coordinates of a point, in contrast to the y-axis mirror (which negates the x-coordinate) and the x-axis mirror (which negates the y-coordinate); they connected this to the anchoring phenomenon by articulating that any mirror line — whether Amina's physical bedroom mirror, the matatu side mirror, or a line on the Cartesian plane — imposes a precise, predictable mathematical rule that determines exactly where the image copy lives.

LESSONS.title: Finding the Mirror Line: Reverse Reflection on Plane Surfaces and the Cartesian Plane

slo.purpose: Learners work backwards from a known object and its image to construct or identify the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each pair of corresponding points, deepening their understanding of all reflection properties simultaneously.
slo.knowledge: The learner knows that: (i) the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its corresponding image point; (ii) this relationship holds on both a plain surface and the Cartesian plane; (iii) the mirror line can be uniquely determined from any single pair of corresponding points.
slo.skills: The learner is able to: (i) construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment joining corresponding object–image points to locate the mirror line on a plain surface; (ii) identify or draw the mirror line on a Cartesian plane given an object and its image; (iii) verify the mirror line by checking that it is equidistant from, and perpendicular to, the line joining every corresponding pair of points.
slo.attitudes: The learner appreciates that the geometric rule governing mirror reflection is precise, reversible, and directly applicable to real-life engineering decisions such as the positioning of road-safety junction mirrors.
slo.keyInquiry: How is reflection important in day-to-day activities?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–5 learners established reflection properties and drew images given objects and mirror lines. Lesson 6 reverses the task: given the object and image, learners must reconstruct the invisible mirror line — the same challenge faced by traffic engineers who must determine exactly where to mount a junction mirror so that a driver (object) can see a specific road hazard (image). This reverse-engineering lens reframes the driving question: the 'perfect copy' in the mirror is governed by a precise geometric rule, and knowing that rule lets us place mirrors deliberately, not just observe them passively.
slo.safetyNotes: Ensure all geometrical instruments (compasses, rulers) are handled carefully. No sharp-instrument injuries during construction activities. Learners working in pairs should share instruments without snatching.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting the Nairobi bedroom-mirror and matatu-mirror phenomenon and are challenged with a new puzzle: if you can see the reflection but the mirror has been removed, can you reconstruct exactly where it stood? Through a structured Predict–Observe–Explain–DQB–Model sequence, learners use compass-and-ruler construction (and coordinate geometry on the Cartesian plane) to find mirror lines as perpendicular bisectors of object–image segments. The road-safety junction-mirror scenario grounds the abstract construction in an authentic Kenyan engineering context. By the end of the lesson, learners can both construct the mirror line on plain paper and identify it algebraically on the Cartesian plane, completing the full two-way mastery of reflection.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a plain A4 sheet on which two congruent triangles (labelled ABC and A'B'C') have been pre-drawn in identical orientation but laterally flipped, with no mirror line shown. Learners study the sheet silently for 90 seconds, then write individual responses to three prompts in their exercise books: (1) 'Where do you think the mirror line is — sketch it freehand.' (2) 'What clues in the diagram tell you where the mirror must be?' (3) 'How might a traffic engineer use this same reasoning to position a junction mirror on the Nairobi–Thika highway?' Learners then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes before the teacher takes three cold-call responses.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute pre-drawn sheets before the lesson begins to save time. Project the same diagram on the board using a TDD or drawn on the chalkboard. Read the three prompts aloud slowly, then say: 'You have 90 seconds of silent thinking — no talking, no pencils yet. Just look.' After silent time: 'Now write your three responses. You have 3 minutes.' After writing: 'Turn to your neighbour. Share your sketch and your clues. 2 minutes.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Cold-call: 'Amina — where did you sketch the mirror line and why?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] 'Brian — did your clue agree with Amina's or differ? Tell us one thing that was different.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] 'Zawadi — what did your group say about the traffic engineer question?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Record three different predicted mirror-line positions on the board without correcting them. Say: 'We will return to these predictions at the end of the lesson to see who was closest — and more importantly, why.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction-with-evidence prompting. By requiring learners to articulate the visual clues that locate the mirror line before any instruction, this strategy activates prior knowledge from Lessons 1–5 (distance-preservation, perpendicularity) and creates cognitive dissonance when predictions diverge, motivating the observational phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner sketches show the predicted mirror line passing roughly midway between the two triangles (acceptable range: within the correct half of the page). Listen for use of vocabulary from previous lessons — 'equidistant,' 'perpendicular,' 'midpoint' — as evidence of prior learning transfer. Flag learners whose sketches place the mirror line outside the figure entirely for targeted support in Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Activity A — Plain-surface construction (30 min, pairs): Each pair receives a fresh worksheet showing three separate object–image pairs on plain paper: (i) a single point P and its image P'; (ii) a line segment MN and its image M'N'; (iii) a quadrilateral KLMN and its image K'L'M'N'. Using a ruler and compass, learners: (a) join P to P' and construct the perpendicular bisector — this IS the mirror line; (b) repeat for two pairs of corresponding vertices on MN/M'N' and verify that both perpendicular bisectors are the same line; (c) repeat for two pairs of corresponding vertices on the quadrilateral and check all bisectors coincide. Learners record: the midpoint coordinates (measured with a ruler), the angle between PP' and the mirror line, and the distances from P and P' to the mirror line. Activity B — Cartesian plane task (15 min, individual): Learners are given a Cartesian grid with triangle PQR (P(2,1), Q(4,1), R(3,4)) and its image P'Q'R' (P'(-2,1), Q'(-4,1), R'(-3,4)). They: (a) plot both triangles; (b) join P to P' and find its midpoint; (c) find the equation of the perpendicular bisector; (d) repeat for Q–Q'; (e) confirm the mirror line equation is x = 0. Learners annotate their grid with the mirror line and its equation.
framework.teacherMoves: Before Activity A, model ONE construction step on the board: draw two points X and X', join them, then say: 'Watch carefully — I am going to open my compass to MORE than half of XX'. Set it on X. Draw an arc above and below the line. Now same radius, set it on X'. Two more arcs. Where they cross — THAT is the perpendicular bisector. Why does this give us the mirror line? I want you to figure that out.' [WAIT 15 seconds for silent thinking.] Circulate during pair work. At the 10-minute mark, pause the class: 'Hold up your worksheets — I want to see the construction arcs. If I cannot see arcs, you are measuring instead of constructing — stop and try again.' Targeted question to struggling pairs: 'You said the midpoint is here — measure from your midpoint to P, then to P'. Are they the same? What does that tell you?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Before Activity B, say: 'Now we move to the Cartesian plane. Instead of a compass you will use algebra. The rule is the same — find the midpoint, find the perpendicular. Let's see if the mirror line equation surprises you.' After Activity B, cold-call three learners: 'Kamau — what equation did you get for the mirror line?' [WAIT 10 sec.] 'Fatuma — how did you check it was correct?' [WAIT 10 sec.] 'Otieno — does this mirror line match any line we have worked with before in this unit?' [WAIT 12 sec.] Connect to phenomenon: 'This is exactly what a traffic engineer does at a junction on Waiyaki Way — she knows where the driver sits and where the hazard is, so she solves for the mirror position mathematically.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked-example fading with reverse task structure. The teacher provides one full construction model, then learners complete progressively more complex cases independently. The deliberate reversal of the standard task (finding the image FROM the mirror line) to the inverse task (finding the mirror line FROM the image) forces learners to interrogate the underlying geometric relationship rather than follow a procedure, building conceptual depth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Construction arcs are visible and intersect correctly — absence of arcs indicates procedural shortcutting; address immediately. (2) Measured distances from object and image to the constructed mirror line are equal (tolerance: ±1 mm) — unequal distances indicate a construction error. (3) On the Cartesian task, the mirror line equation x = 0 is identified correctly and the midpoint of PP' is calculated as (0, 1) — wrong midpoints suggest coordinate arithmetic errors. Use mini-whiteboards or scrap paper for learners to show midpoint calculations for a quick whole-class scan.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole-class sensemaking discussion (10 min): The teacher projects (or draws) a summary diagram showing an object point A, its image A', the segment AA', its midpoint M, and the perpendicular bisector through M labelled as the mirror line ℓ. Learners are asked to articulate in their own words the complete logical chain: 'Why must the mirror line be EXACTLY the perpendicular bisector — not just any line through M?' Pairs discuss for 90 seconds, then three pairs share. Application task — Junction Mirror Problem (10 min, individual): Learners receive a printed map-style diagram (Kenya road-junction context) showing: a driver's eye position D(1, 3) and a road hazard H(-5, 3) on a Cartesian grid. They must find the equation of the mirror line that would allow the driver to see the hazard in a junction mirror — i.e., find the perpendicular bisector of DH. Learners write a two-sentence 'real-world interpretation' beneath their working: 'The mirror should be placed along the line x = __ because …'
framework.teacherMoves: Open the discussion: 'Before you tell me the answer, I want the REASON. Zawadi — if the mirror line just passed through the midpoint but was NOT perpendicular, what would go wrong with the reflection?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Accept and probe responses. Say: 'The key word I want everyone to use in their explanation is EQUIDISTANT. The mirror line is the set of all points equidistant from the object and its image. Say that with me.' [Choral repetition.] 'Now write it in your book in your own words — 30 seconds.' For the Junction Mirror Problem, say: 'You are now the traffic engineer hired by Kenya Roads Board. Show your working as if you are writing a report. I need the equation of the mirror line AND one sentence explaining what it means physically.' Circulate and read two or three written interpretations aloud (anonymised) for class discussion. Cold-call: 'Brian — you wrote that the mirror should be at x = −2. Walk us through your midpoint calculation.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] 'Amina — does Brian's answer match the diagram? How do you know?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Explicitly connect back to the phenomenon: 'Remember the matatu side mirror we discussed in Lesson 1? The engineer who designed the mirror mount solved exactly this kind of equation — they knew the driver's seat position and the danger zone position, and they found the mirror line mathematically.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Reasoning-aloud with targeted vocabulary scaffolding. By requiring learners to articulate the logical chain using the term 'equidistant' and to write a real-world interpretation, the strategy consolidates procedural skill into conceptual understanding and links the abstract algebraic result to the anchoring phenomenon, making the mathematics meaningful rather than mechanical.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner explanations include both 'midpoint' and 'perpendicular' (or 'equidistant') — responses using only one term indicate partial understanding. (2) Junction Mirror equation is x = −2 (midpoint of (1,3) and (−5,3) is (−2,3); perpendicular bisector of a horizontal segment is a vertical line x = −2) — arithmetic errors in midpoint calculation are the most common failure mode; watch for learners averaging y-coordinates instead of x-coordinates. (3) Written real-world interpretations mention both the driver and the hazard, not just the equation — purely procedural responses indicate the phenomenon connection has not been made.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes on a sticky note (or a designated section of their exercise book if sticky notes are unavailable) ONE new understanding and ONE remaining question prompted by today's lesson. They post or record these under two columns on the class DQB: 'What we now know' and 'What we still wonder.' The class then does a 3-minute silent gallery read of all posted notes. Three learners are cold-called to read aloud one 'still wonder' note that resonates with them and to suggest which future lesson might address it. The teacher annotates the DQB to show which questions will be answered in Lessons 7 and 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'At the start of this unit our driving question was: Why does a mirror show a perfect copy of the world — and where exactly does that copy live? On your sticky note, write: first — one thing you can now answer about that question that you could not answer in Lesson 1; second — one thing that still puzzles you.' [Allow 3 minutes writing time.] 'Stand up, post your note, then read three notes from classmates in silence. 3 minutes.' After gallery read, cold-call: 'Otieno — read one 'still wonder' note that you found interesting.' [WAIT 10 sec.] 'Fatuma — can you guess which lesson might answer that question?' [WAIT 10 sec.] 'Kamau — has today's lesson changed your answer to the driving question compared to what you wrote in Lesson 1? How?' [WAIT 12 sec.] Point to the board: 'Our model of reflection is nearly complete. Lesson 7 will tackle reflections in the lines y = 0 and y = x on the Cartesian plane, and Lesson 8 will bring everything together in a real road-safety design task.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Metacognitive DQB curation. Requiring learners to distinguish between resolved and unresolved questions makes their growing understanding visible to themselves and to the teacher. The gallery-read ritual builds collective sense of progress and sustains curiosity for remaining lessons, maintaining the storyline coherence of the eight-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) 'What we now know' statements reference the perpendicular bisector relationship specifically — vague statements like 'mirrors work in a special way' indicate surface-level understanding. (2) 'Still wonder' questions are conceptually forward-looking (e.g., 'What happens when the mirror line is y = x?') rather than procedurally backward (e.g., 'How do I use a compass?') — procedural questions signal that Phase 2 consolidation was incomplete and require teacher follow-up. (3) Cold-call responses demonstrate ability to link today's learning to the original driving question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative 'Reflection Model' diagram that they have been building since Lesson 1 (a growing annotated diagram showing the mirror, the object, the image, and labelled properties). They add a new layer to the model: (a) draw a double-headed arrow between any object point and its image point, label the midpoint as lying ON the mirror line, and annotate 'mirror line = perpendicular bisector of every object–image segment'; (b) add a new box to their model's legend: 'REVERSE TASK: given object + image → construct mirror line using perpendicular bisector method'; (c) annotate the road-safety inset (a small junction-mirror sketch they added in Lesson 3) with today's equation-based method, showing that the mirror line position can be calculated from known positions of driver and hazard. Pairs compare their updated models and identify any inconsistency with properties recorded in earlier lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Reflection Model from your portfolio. Today's lesson adds the final missing direction arrow — we can now go both ways: object → image AND image → object → mirror line. Add the new annotation now. You have 5 minutes.' [Circulate, checking that the perpendicular bisector annotation is correctly placed and that the road-safety inset is updated.] After 5 minutes: 'Swap models with your partner. Check: does their perpendicular bisector annotation match the properties we verified today? Does their road-safety inset use the correct equation method? Write one positive comment and one suggestion on a sticky note.' [Allow 3 minutes.] Cold-call final reflection: 'Amina — looking at your complete model from Lessons 1 to 6, what is the single most important geometric idea that explains everything the mirror does?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] 'Brian — how would you explain to the matatu driver why his side mirror shows vehicles that appear behind him but seem to be at the same distance as they really are?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Close with the phenomenon link: 'Next lesson we will extend our model to mirror lines that are not just vertical or horizontal — and we will discover a new surprise about the line y = x.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer audit. The physical act of annotating and then peer-auditing the cumulative model externalises understanding, makes conceptual growth tangible over the lesson sequence, and creates accountability for precision. Connecting the algebraic result to the road-safety inset already present in the model reinforces the phenomenon thread across all six lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The perpendicular bisector annotation is correctly placed on the model with both the midpoint label and the right-angle symbol — missing either element indicates incomplete understanding of the two-part condition. (2) The road-safety inset shows an equation (e.g., x = −2) derived from the midpoint method, not just a freehand sketch — purely sketch-based updates indicate the algebraic method from Phase 3 has not been internalised. (3) Peer-audit sticky notes identify genuine mathematical inconsistencies rather than cosmetic comments — superficial comments ('nice diagram') suggest learners are not yet auditing for mathematical correctness; prompt with 'find one number or label to check.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Did the reverse-task framing (finding the mirror line from the object and image) genuinely produce more conceptual discussion than forward tasks in Lessons 3–5, or did learners default to procedural compass use without articulating the perpendicular bisector reasoning? Note specific moments where the 'equidistant' vocabulary did or did not appear spontaneously. (2) In Activity B (Cartesian plane), did learners transfer the geometric construction reasoning into the algebraic midpoint-and-perpendicular method independently, or did they require significant scaffolding? Identify any learners who could do the plain-surface construction but could not set up the algebraic version — plan a bridging task for Lesson 7. (3) Was the Junction Mirror Problem (Kenya Roads Board scenario) sufficiently contextualised? Did learners write genuine real-world interpretations or merely re-state the equation? If interpretations were shallow, consider displaying a photograph of an actual Kenyan junction mirror (e.g., at a T-junction in Westlands, Nairobi) at the start of Lesson 7 to deepen the phenomenon connection. (4) Review the DQB 'still wonder' notes: are there patterns in remaining confusion (e.g., questions about non-vertical mirror lines, or about three-dimensional reflections) that should be pre-addressed in Lesson 7's predict phase? (5) Were lesson timings realistic? The construction activity is ambitious for 30 minutes — if pairs did not complete all three worksheet cases, prioritise cases (i) and (iii) in Lesson 7 warm-up review.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed that when two congruent, laterally-flipped figures are drawn with no mirror line, the perpendicular bisectors of segments joining corresponding points all coincide at a single line — the mirror line — on both plain paper (via compass construction) and the Cartesian plane (via midpoint and perpendicular equation). They also observed that this reverse-engineering method can determine the exact placement of a junction mirror given the positions of a driver and a road hazard.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its corresponding image point; that this property holds universally on plain surfaces and the Cartesian plane; that the mirror line can be constructed geometrically using compass arcs or determined algebraically by finding the midpoint and the equation of the perpendicular line; and that this mathematical rule underpins the real-world positioning of road-safety mirrors by traffic engineers in Kenya.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained why the mirror line must be both the midpoint locus AND perpendicular to each object–image segment — it is the set of all points equidistant from the object and its image, meaning any other line through the midpoint would produce a different, non-congruent image. They connected this reasoning to the anchoring phenomenon (the Nairobi bedroom mirror and matatu side mirrors) and to the junction-mirror engineering context, articulating that the 'invisible rule' governing where the reflection lives is the perpendicular bisector relationship, discoverable in both directions of the reflection task.
